### 1.1 Seven Principles of Universal Design
The seven Principles of Universal Design (National Disability Authority 2012) were developed to guide the design of environments, products, and communications.

#### 1.1.1 Principle 1: Equitable Use The design should be useful and marketable to people with diverse abilities. Guidelines:
• Provide the same means of use for all users: identical whenever possible; equivalent when not. • Avoid segregating or stigmatizing any users. • Provisions for privacy, security, and safety should be equally available to all users. • Make the design appealing to all users. • Ensure dignity in use for all users.

#### 1.1.2 Principle 2: Flexibility in Use The design should accommodate a wide range of individual preferences and abilities. Guidelines:
• Provide choice in methods of use. • Accommodate right- or left-handed access and use. • Facilitate the user's accuracy and precision. • Provide adaptability to the user's pace.

#### 1.1.3 Principle 3: Simple and Intuitive Use Use of the design should be easy to understand, regardless of the user's experience, knowledge, language skills, or current concentration level. Guidelines:
• Eliminate unnecessary complexity. • Be consistent with user expectations and intuition. • Accommodate a wide range of literacy and language skills. • Arrange information consistent with its importance. • Provide effective prompting and feedback during and after task completion.

#### 1.1.4 Principle 4: Perceptible Information The design should communicate necessary information effectively to the user, regardless of ambient conditions or the user's sensory abilities. Guidelines:
• Use different modes (pictorial, verbal, tactile) for redundant presentation of essential information. • Provide adequate contrast between essential information and its surroundings. • Maximize "legibility" of essential information. • Differentiate elements in ways that can be described (i.e., make it easy to give instructions or directions). • Provide compatibility with a variety of techniques or devices used by people with sensory limitations. Page 7 of 31

#### 1.1.5 Principle 5: Tolerance for Error The design should minimise hazards and the adverse consequences of accidental or unintended actions. Guidelines:
• Arrange elements to minimize hazards and errors: most used elements, most accessible; hazardous elements eliminated, isolated, or shielded. • Provide warnings of hazards and errors. • Provide fail safe features. • Discourage unconscious action in tasks that require vigilance.

#### 1.1.6 Principle 6: Low Physical Effort The design should be sufficient such that it can be used efficiently and comfortably and with a minimum of fatigue. Guidelines:
• Allow user to maintain a neutral body position. • Use reasonable operating forces. • Minimize repetitive actions. • Minimize sustained physical effort. 1.1.7 Principle 7: Size and Space for Approach and Use Appropriate size and space must be provided for approach, reach, manipulation, and use regardless of user's body size, posture, or mobility. Guidelines: • Provide a clear line of sight to important elements for any seated or standing user. • Make reach to all components comfortable for any seated or standing user. • Accommodate variations in hand and grip size. • Provide adequate space for the use of assistive devices or personal assistance.

### 1.2 The social model of disability
These guidelines are informed by the Social Model of Disability (Oliver 1990, Scope n.d.). This proposes that the majority of disability is caused by a lack of accommodation for impairments and differences. For example, a wheelchair user cannot get into a building because there are steps before the entrance. This is disabling not because the person is using a wheelchair but due to a lack of provision of a ramp. The responsibility for access lies with the owners of the building, not with the disabled person. “Barriers can make it impossible or very difficult to access jobs, buildings or services, but the biggest barrier of all is the problem of people’s attitude to disability. Removing the barriers is the best way to include millions of disabled people in our society” (TUC 2019).

### 1.3 The duty to make reasonable adjustments
All employers have a legal duty under the Equality Act 2010 to proactively make reasonable adjustments to remove, reduce or prevent any disadvantages that disabled workers face (TUC 2019). In order to achieve equity for disabled people, work may need to be organised differently, support provided, and barriers removed. Page 8 of 31

### 1.4 The benefits of accessible labs
Labs are often designed without consideration to disability access due to the historic assumption that disabled scientists could not work safely in such environments. If disabled people’s needs are not designed into work and workplaces, then few disabled people will be able to work there. This is part of why there is a significant under representation of disabled people working in science, technology, engineering, and maths (STEM). Whilst approximately 22% of the UK adult population of working age are disabled, only around 3.8% of UK STEM academics are identified as disabled (Joice 2021). The lack of diversity in research participants and scientists is a factor in wasteful research due to serious flaws in prioritisation, design, sampling, analysis and interpretation, etc. (Glasziou 2018; Macleod 2014; JLA 2023). Research that is informed by a diverse multidisciplinary team is better able to ensure practicality, utility, and impact (Deane 2014 and 2019, Schroeder 2022). The opportunity cost of not having disabled scientists with their diversity of experience and expertise is likely to be significant. Additionally, most disabilities are acquired; the loss of highly qualified scientists from the field when they acquire a disability is a substantial loss on the investment in their training. We start with the assumption that all disabled scientists are able to work in labs, if the labs are designed with their access needs met. Safety issues can be designed “out” of the labs; either in the structural or equipment design or in the protocols used. Accessibility also includes the design of the work processes, staff knowledge and attitudes. Accessible labs will allow a greater proportion of disabled scientists to be trained and work in lab settings in a safe and comfortable manner. We genuinely believe this improved diversity in the workforce will enhance the quality and potential profitability of the work done in laboratory settings. Page 9 of 31

## 2 Key Access Considerations
There are detailed specifications below, but the key access considerations and solutions can be grouped as follows.

### 2.1 Mobility
1 Wheelchair users need space. Always provide generous turning circles etc, as tight spaces mean damage e.g., to doorways and wheelchairs. Additionally, whilst a single wheelchair user will usually take up “2 people spaces”, when two wheelchair users are in a single space they will need around “6 people spaces” in order to circulate freely. 2. Grab rails must be provided anywhere someone might transfer from a wheelchair. Consider if a hoist might be appropriate. 3. Consider providing to two fire safe lifts per building. (Allows for redundancy in event of maintenance or faults). 4. Wherever possible specify lifts and toilets of a minimum size that will accommodate room for a carer to be able to assist the wheelchair user.

### 2.2 Dexterity and strength
1 All taps should be lever type. 2. All doors should be light. 3. Door handles and locks should allow easy grip and have good colour contrast

### 2.3 Sensory
1 Good colour contrast, matt surfaces. 2. Good lighting. 3. Signs and alarms should have two modes e.g., audible and visual fire alarms, visual and tactile signs. 4. Create a good auditory environment with sound baffles etc. 5. Hearing technology must be provided. 6. Microphones must be provided in meeting spaces.

### 2.4 Toilets etc.
1 Provide accessible toilets that are as large as possible on every floor. 2. Consider providing a Changing Place (CP) accessible toilet in the building’s foyer. 3. If facilities are provided where people change clothes, a hoist should be considered. Page 10 of 31

### 3.1 Visual Access: Colours
Contrasting colours should be used to distinguish once thing from another; a difference of at least 30 points in light reflectance value (BS8300-2 2018). • Different colours for floors and walls and doors. • Different colours for work surfaces (which should be matt) from walls. • Handles should be a different colour from doors. • Face plates for sockets and light switches should be a contrasting colour compared to the switch and the wall. Choice of colours and contrasts should consider colour blindness etc. Flooring and door mats must never be black. For some people with dementia or visual impairments this looks like a hole. Care should be taken with patterns on floors. For some visual impairments patterns can create false movement and depth and may negatively impact on gait stability. The contrast strip should be on the edge of any steps (not before it). The contrast strip will have a high level of visual contrast.

### 3.2 Visual Access: Lighting
All office and meeting room spaces should have natural light where possible. Flexible lighting options should be provided with a view to light spectrum, light intensity, and window blinds. Lighting must be sufficient and not create glare. Bare bulbs are to be avoided. Translucent covers to diffuse lights are recommended. Harsh strip lighting is not appropriate. Flexible lighting to focus on the face of the presenter (so lip-reading is enhanced) and on a sign language interpreter in meeting room settings. The emergency lighting levels need to be greater level than normally required by building control in order to facilitate safe evacuation of disabled persons (Building Standards 2010). • In high-risk buildings a minimum of 15 lux is required • In medium and low to risk buildings a minimum of 10 lux is required

### 3.3 Hearing Access: Acoustic adjustments
Acoustic adjustments are complex (BS8233 2014) and may require specialist advice on installation. Consideration should be given to the acoustic noisiness of areas where many people have conversations i.e., foyers, canteens, meeting rooms. Consideration should be given to sound proofing between rooms. Page 11 of 31 Consideration should be given to the use of sound baffles in acoustically reflective environments i.e., areas with a lot of hard surfaces. Consideration should be given to the background noise level of equipment e.g., ventilation, hoods, alarms etc.

### 3.4 Hearing Access: Hearing loops and other hearing technologies
Reception desks must have hearing loops. Hearing loops or similar technology should be provided in all laboratories, meeting rooms and offices. Exact specification will be determined according to room type and acceptability of solutions to the person with hearing access needs. Consideration should be given to lines of sight, colours, lighting levels and space sufficient for someone to use sign language or lip reading for communication. Personal hearing aids or noise reduction aids are discussed in Protocol Access Guidelines (Deane 2023a)

### 3.5 Floors
Flooring both internal and external should be non-slip (even when wet). Flooring should be smooth and give low resistance to rolling. Flooring should contrast in colour with the walls (a difference of at least 30 points in light reflectance value, BS8300-2 2018). Flooring should not “turn up” the wall without a colour change. Door mats should be a similar colour to surrounding floor. They should be long enough to allow wheelchair wheels to fully dry off on entry into a building (minimum 2000mm long, BS8300-2 section 8.6.1 (2018)). Flooring and door mats must never be black. For some people with dementia or visual impairments this looks like a hole. Care should be taken with patterns on floors. For some visual impairments patterns can create false movement and depth and may negatively impact on gait stability.

### 3.6 Glass partitions
There must be clear visual markings on all glass partitions, walls, barriers etc, at both standing and sitting height i.e., from 850 mm to 1000 mm from the floor and from 1400 mm to 1600 mm from the floor (BS8300-2 section 11.5 (2018)).

### 3.7 Corridors
The minimum space required for two wheelchair users to pass each other on an access route is 1800 mm (BS8300-2 section 9.1 (2018)).

### 3.8 Steps and stairs
Page 12 of 31 If possible, steps should be removed from the design (except for protected stairs between floors). Steps with associated ramps are acceptable (please note that steps may aid the mobility of those using leg prostheses for whom ramps can be problematic). Ground floor fire escape routes should never include steps. Fire exit steps and staircases must be straight to allow for the use of Evacuation Chairs. Where fire safe lifts cannot be installed (or only one can be installed) then ideally staircases should be large enough to allow for the use of a portable powered wheelchair evacuation platform and stair climber that can accommodate manual or electric wheelchairs (e.g., Super Trac 2021). This model requires 1600mm x 1600mm clearance. All steps need handrails on both sides. External handrails must not be bare metal. The contrast strip should be on the edge of the step (not before it). The contrast strip will have a high level of visual contrast. Consideration should be given to a different colour contrasting strip on the first and last steps of each flight. Stair risers should be solid (no floating stairs). Glass must not be used for the step or riser of stairs. Great care should be used when considering the use of glass for the sides of stairways. Consideration should be given to putting a lip on the side edges of steps where there are gaps between the step and the wall – to prevent sticks and crutches from slipping off the step. Consideration should be given to recessed lighting of steps (see lighting section).

### 3.9 Fire Alarms and Refuges
Fire alarms should include a visual alarm (flashing light) in addition to the auditory alarm. Refuge point alarms should be clearly sign posted and instructions for use posted (Home Office 2007). Refuge points must be located such that the noise generated by the fire alarm system does not prevent easy communication between the refuge point and whoever is responding.

### 3.10 Lifts
The smallest acceptable size of lift is 1100 mm wide × 1400 mm deep. This allows one wheelchair user and one accompanying person but does not allow a chair to turn around (BS8300-2 section 10.5 (2018)). Ideally a lift should be large enough to allow a wheelchair user to turn around (i.e., 1500mm turning circle) (BS8300-2 section 10.5 (2018)). Stair lifts must be at least 1100 mm wide × 1400 mm deep (but ideally larger as this size does not accommodate a carer) and carry 300Kg minimum – with consideration given to increasing this to 400kg where possible. Page 13 of 31 Signage in lifts should be large, clear and contrasting and include braille. Auditory messages must be provided to inform users of floor levels and door opening and closing. Lighting should be bright enough to allow reading of signs. Care will be taken to ensure that the lights do not create glare e.g., by using frosted covers for downlighters, matt surfaces on signage. Mirrors recommended in all lifts to facilitate safe reversing out by wheelchair users. They are essential in older, smaller lifts which do not have space for a turning circle. The flooring of the lift should contrast visually with the landing flooring but should not be black – for some people with dementia or visual impairments this looks like a hole. A lift’s location in the building should be clearly signed. Consideration should be given to location of lifts with regards to access to lifts out of hours and at weekends. Consideration should be given to the provision of more than one lift in a building to allow for repairs, maintenance, and break downs. Lifts should be installed as full evacuation lifts to BS9999 (2017) i.e., they can be used to evacuate mobility impaired staff in the event of fire. Where possible refurbishment of old lifts should be to BS9999 (2017).

### 3.11 Doors
Must be accessible for all users i.e., they must be light, held open, or powered. Doorways should be wide enough (800 mm minimum – but more detailed guidance available from BS8300-2 section 8.3 (2018)). Doors should be as light as possible to open. Consider removing unneeded door closers. Consider installing low friction bearings on hinges. For non-fire-resisting doors, rising butt hinges can be used to close door (BS8300-2 section 9 (2018)) Corridor doors should be kept open with magnets (so they close in the event of fire), or power assisted. All heavy doors should be power assisted. (Heavy is >30 N force to open, Building Standard 2010). Consideration should be given to the best location of the push pads for the doors. If an assistance dog is trained to push these pads it may be helpful to install a second linked pad at a lower height for the dog to push. Grab rails and handles should not be cold (i.e., bare metal). All lever and pull handles should be of suitable dimensions and clearance (BS8300-2 section 8.4 (2018)) All door locks should use large simple to use levers. A suitable lock can be identified as one that can be operated with a closed fist. This includes the locks in standard toilets. Page 14 of 31

### 3.12 Services and controls
To assist wheelchair users who have reduced reach, services and controls should comply with all of the following. Consumer units should be mounted so that the switches are between 1350mm and 1450mm above floor level. (Building Regulations 2010) Switches, sockets, stopcocks and controls, except controls to radiators, are located with their centre line 700-1000mm above floor level and a minimum of 700mm (measured horizontally) from an inside corner and are not positioned behind appliances. (Building Regulations 2010) Power isolators should be located within the same height range. (Building Regulations 2010) Consideration should be given to the location of switches. Ideally, they will be reachable from a wheelchair or by someone of restricted growth, and not require reaching above shoulder height. They should not require reaching over hot plates, water baths etc. If the workspace has windows that open, then the handle to at least one window in the principal working area is 700-1000mm above floor level, unless fitted with a remote opening device that is within this height range (Building Regulations 2010) Handles to all other windows are 450-1200mm above floor level, unless the window is fitted with a remote opening device that is within this height range (Building Regulations 2010) Door handles, locks, latches and catches are both: • easy to grip and use, and • fitted 850-1000mm above floor level (Building Regulations 2010). Light switches are on individual plates unless wide rocker or full plate fittings are provided (Building Regulations 2010). Switches to double socket outlets are located at the outer ends of the plate (rather than in the centre) (Building Regulations 2010). Light switches and power sockets should have a contrasting colour fascia or be outlined with a contrasting colour paint line (a difference of at least 30 points in light reflectance value, BS8300-2 (2018)). Many people with disabilities use equipment that needs to be recharged regularly. Accessible offices should have approximately twice the usual number of sockets provided. Detailed guidance on making equipment accessible is provided in our separate Equipment Access Guidelines (Deane 2023b). Equipment controls should: • have with clearly defined controls (contrasting colours and/or tactile difference) • controls that do not require strength or dexterity • controls that can be used from a seated and standing position Consideration should be given to controls that can be linked to external access solutions e.g., large touch screens, voice activated controls etc. Page 15 of 31 Consideration to be given to provision of equipment that gives audible speech output of the functions chosen.

### 3.13 Air Ventilation and Temperature
Many disabled people are at high risk from airborne infections (e.g., Covid-19), and are more sensitive to room temperatures, both high and low. The highest standards of ventilation should be achieved i.e., target CO2 concentrations below 800ppm or typically 10 l/s/person (CIBSE 2021). Consideration should be given to air cleaning e.g., HEPA filters or UV light treatment – particularly in enclosed spaces where outside ventilation is inappropriate (CIBSE 2021). The ability to change the temperature of an area should be included.

### 3.14 Taps and Sinks
All taps in all locations must be lever taps or automatic taps. This includes taps in standard toilets and all kitchens, and gas taps in laboratories. Hand wash sinks in laboratories must be placed at an appropriate height for people standing and people in wheelchairs. Sinks in kitchens and laboratories must use lever taps or sensors located so that they can be reached by a wheelchair user. Taps must be a contrasting colour to their surroundings.

### 3.15 Lab furniture and equipment
See also Equipment Access Guidelines (Deane 2023b). In laboratories variable height work benches, fume hoods, and microbiological safety cabinets must be provided. Consideration should be given to placing large equipment (e.g., incubators) on variable height stands. Benches should ideally have 1800mm between them; the absolute minimum gap is 1530mm. This allows people to sit on chairs at each bench and still have sufficient space for a wheelchair to roll behind the chairs without knocking into them. Staff should be allocated a minimum of 1500mm width per workstation on the bench. Consideration should be given to the inclusion of knee hole spaces for wheelchair users and those who need to sit whilst working in the lab e.g., in a run of floor level cupboards. NB. These spaces must be kept clear (they are not a space for bins or storage). Consideration should be given to the provision of pull-down shelving for wall cupboards and pull out or carousel shelving in floor level cupboards. Door handles on cupboards, fridges, freezers, incubators etc. should be able to be gripped all the way around – to accommodate poor dexterity or limited strength. These handles should be of a contrasting colour. Page 16 of 31

### 3.16 General furniture
Consideration should be made for flexibility of use. Choose chairs with a consideration to ergonomic design and lower lumbar support. If chairs are stackable, they must have hand holes in back of chairs. Variable height tables and desks must be provided. Manual cranks may be superior to electric motors in terms of both cost and reliability. Consideration should be given to using lightweight furniture, particularly if it is expected to be moved. If it is unavoidably heavy, then consideration should be given to putting it on lockable wheels. Lockable wheels on lightweight tables and chairs allow for ease of movement but also stability when in place. Consideration should be given to the positioning of furniture to allow for ease of movement between it of those walking and/or using wheelchairs e.g., at least 1200mm between groups of chairs. Lockable storage should be available to store medications that need to be kept at room temperature, disability aids, clothing etc. Consideration should be given to ease of access from a wheelchair, and the dexterity required to operate handles and locks. Fridges should be provided outside of lab area for medications or prescribed foods that require refrigeration. Lockable boxes should be available to store refrigerated medications.

### 3.17 Navigation and Information
For neurodiverse staff the provision of a clock is very helpful to manage time. Make sure it does not tick. Signage should highlight accessible routes, doors, lifts. Signs should use both words and symbols to indicate where toilets and lifts are. Sans serif font, clear contrast between background and text, suitable size font (particularly if it needs to be read from standing), coloured background preferred (see Dissemination Access Guidelines for further details (Deane 2023d)). Consideration should be given to location and height of signs, so they are suitable to be read from standing and sitting positions. Web pages should provide detailed information on access throughout all buildings and surrounding spaces (see Dissemination Access Guidelines for further details (Deane 2023d)). Consideration should be given to the provision of QR codes or similar on key pieces of equipment or locations, to allow for additional information / navigation assistance to be provided via mobile phones. Page 17 of 31 Information should be updated when routes or rooms are blocked (for repairs etc). This information should be provided preferentially to disabled staff e.g., via text alerts, emails.

### 3.18 Meeting Rooms
Microphones and slide controls must not be fixed in place. Where a podium is provided it should: • Have sufficient space behind it for a wheelchair to manoeuvre • Have separate lighting onto the podium • Provide wireless keyboard and mouse or sufficient cable length on keyboard and mouse to allow for their use across the entire width of the podium • Have a computer screen that can be adjusted for height and angle • Have a microphone that can be angled to be used from a wheelchair to the side of the podium • Be as light as possible and be on lockable wheels

### 3.19 Quiet Spaces
Consideration should be given to designing quiet spaces into building plans. These should have space for a couple of people to sit and for one person to lie down. There should be space for a wheelchair turning circle (1500mm) once the furniture is installed. There should be comfortable seating and a bench to allow someone to lie down. Consideration should be given to providing lights that are adjustable in brightness. Consideration should be given to the soundproofing of such a room. The door of the room should have a vacant/engaged sign and have a lever lock to ensure privacy e.g., when breastfeeding.

### 3.20 Assistance dog toilets/spending areas
Assistance dog toilets or spending areas should be provided to allow people who use assistance dogs to toilet their dogs in a safe and clean manner. An enclosed space of 3000mm x 4000mm that is wheelchair accessible is recommended. More details available in the guidance from Guide Dogs for The Blind Association, 2015.

### 3.21 Toilets and Shower Rooms
Workplaces should provide suitable toilet and washing facilities. Reasonable provision will vary depending on the number of employees and visitors a space is expected to accommodate. If possible, an accessible toilet should be provided on every floor of the building. If possible, a Changing Place (CP) Toilet should be provided in the ground floor foyer of the building. (See later for specification of CP Toilets). Workplaces should aspire to provide spacious facilities that can accommodate a variety of needs e.g., larger wheelchairs, the need to transfer from both sides, or the need for a wheelchair user to Page 18 of 31 also have a carer providing assistance. Additionally, workplaces have to provide bins for general waste, sanitary towels, and sanitary pads, and these can take up a fair amount of floor space. The door to the toilet facility opens outwards. Provide a minimum 1500mm clear turning circle. But this is the absolute minimum and if a larger turning circle can be provided it should be. The turning circle should not be obstructed by bins, changing tables etc. The door opening arc should not impinge on the turning circle (Building Regulations 2010). All walls, ducts and boxings to every toilet/cloakroom, bath and shower room are strong enough to support grab rails, seats and other adaptations that could impose a load of 1.5kN/m2. The loading for strengthened walls is considered suitable for many types of adaptations but additional localised strengthening may be required if adaptations are fitted that impose high point loads (Building Regulations 2010). The ceiling structure to bathrooms and toilet/cloakrooms is strong enough to allow for the fitting of an overhead hoist capable of carrying a load of 200kg (Building Regulations 2010). Where sanitary facilities are wheelchair accessible, toilet flush controls are positioned on the front of the cistern on the transfer side and can be easily gripped, e.g., a lever flush handle (Building Regulations 2010). Where sanitary facilities are wheelchair accessible, toilet pans should be a minimum of 400mm high. Where sanitary facilities are wheelchair accessible, basins and sinks should be wall hung (typically with their rim 770-850mm above finished floor level) and the clear zone beneath basins, services and pedestals is maximised to enable wheelchair users to approach. Ideally this clear zone should be in the range 400-600mm from finished floor level (Building Regulations 2010). Stacks or soil and vent pipes should only be positioned adjacent to toilet where there is no practical alternative and should always be on the wall side of the toilet (Building Regulations 2010). All toilet doors should be light (i.e., <30N force to open - see doors) (Building Regulations 2010). This applies to standard as well as accessible toilets. Door closers are unlikely to allow this requirement to be met. If it is wanted for the toilet door to default to a shut position, then rising butt hinges may be useful. Large levers should be provided for locking in all toilets (standard and accessible) i.e., they should be operable using a closed fist (so not much dexterity or strength is required to operate them). Electronic locks are not recommended as they tend to fail too often. Contrasting colours should be used for handrails, toilet seat, tiles behind sink, floor to walls. All taps should be lever taps or automatic taps. This includes taps in standard toilets. Lighting should be motion sensor linked. The red alarm cord should be positioned to the side of the toilet with the greatest space as this where someone is most likely to fall to the floor and need to summon assistance. It is Page 19 of 31 recommended that a card is attached to the red cord explaining its purpose to reduce the risk of them being tied up. For example, Euan’s Guide provides a card that reads “This red emergency cord must hand freely all the way to the floor. If it does not, it many prevent a disabled person from asking for help.” (Euan’s Guide 2015) A shelf for colostomy bags 100mm to 150mm deep and at least 400mm wide should be fitted 950mm above floor level. The shelf should be positioned where it will not obstruct use of the wall mounted handrails or other equipment, but where it is within reach of the person using the toilet (Changing Places Consortium 2015). Full length mirrors should be provided (BS8300-2 2018). This allows users to ensure they are appropriately tidy in their dress before exiting. Signage should be gender neutral where possible and use symbols and words. The signs for accessible toilets should indicate which side you transfer to. Baby changing facilities should be included where possible. However, the extended changing table must not impinge on the 1500mm turning circle or restrict access to other equipment for disabled users. Page 20 of 31 FIGURE 1 - Unisex accessible toilet with corner toilet layout (From BS2300-2 Figures 41 & 42, 2018) Plan View Key 1 Two clothes hooks. One at 1050mm and the other at 1400mm above the floor. 2. Wheelchair turning space 1500mm x 1500mm. 3. Large washbasin with its rim at 780mm to 800mm above floor level, with a mirror above and paper towel dispenser and soap dispenser alongside. 4. See figure below for details of fittings on this side of the room. Key 1 Wall A (see above) 2. Alarm pull cord with two red bangles 3. Vertical grab rails (those above the handwash basin should be set 500mm to 700mm apart centred on the basin). 4. Colostomy changing bag shelf at 950mm above floor level where a high or low level or reduced flush cistern is used. 5. Sanitary dispenser 6. Automatic hand dryer 7. Soap dispenser 8. Paper towel dispenser 9. Toilet paper dispenser Elevation View 10 Alarm reset button 11 Centre line of vertical grab rails 12 Horizontal grab rail 13 Shelf 14 Hand rinse basin with tap on side closest to toilet 15 Flat top closed-coupled cistern providing a back rest and colostomy bag changing surface for standing users. Page 21 of 31

### 3.22 Showers and changing areas
Showers may be needed to allow employees to wash up before work e.g., if they have cycled in. Or a shower may be required to meet decontamination or clean room requirements. Consideration should be made to making these spaces as accessible as possible. Detailed specifications are available in BS2300-2 (2018). Key requirements include: • The shower area should be created as a wet room. • Step free access • A drop-down shower seat with grab rails Changing areas should be provided if personnel are expected to change their apparel. Detailed specification is available from BS2300-2 part 18.3 (2018). Key requirements include Seating should be provided. A drop-down seat with grab rails is best practice. But even a bench with arm rests can be beneficial. Storage lockers should be easy to access from standing or seated positions with lever locks. A fixed “step over” bench or raised sill should not be installed if wheelchair access is required. A lightweight moveable bench or change in the colour of the flooring and walls may aid personnel to identify the clean zone. Consideration should be given to provision of a hoist if full change of apparel is required. If clean room requirements mean that separate clean wheelchair or mobility aids are used, then consideration should be given to a suitable secure storage space with a charging point. Page 22 of 31 FIGURE 2 Self-contained unisex shower room for independent use (From BS2300-2 Figure 38, 2018) Elevation view Plan view 1 Vertical rod to carry a detachable shower head, adjustable within a range 1050mm to 1850mm above the floor. 2. Soap tray 3. Back rest 4. Height range for shower controls 750mm to 1000mm above the floor. 5. Drop down support rails on side and rear walls 6. Tip up shower seat 7. Alarm reset button 8 Towel rail 9. Alarm pull cord 10. Horizontal grab rail 11. Floor drain 12. Vertical grab rail 13. Fall to floor drain not steeper than 1:50 14. Shower curtain 15. Full length mirror 16. Two clothes hooks. One at 1050mm and the other at 1400mm above the floor. Page 23 of 31 FIGURE 3 Self-contained changing area and accessories (from BS 8300-2 Figure 37, 2018) Elevation view Plan view Key 1 Minimum unobstructed room height 2. Vertical grab rail 3. Back rest 4. Two clothes hooks. One at 1050mm and the other at 1400mm above the floor. 5. Towel rail 6 Tip up seat 7. Drop down support rails on side and far wall 8. Alarm reset button (located immediately above backplate of the horizontal grab rail). 9. Horizontal grab rail 10. Alarm pull cord Page 24 of 31

### 3.23 Changing Place Toilets
Changing Place (CP) toilets are designed for people who cannot use a standard accessible toilet. They should be provided in addition to single or gender-neutral toilets, standard accessible toilets and baby changing facilities. CP toilets are designed for people who need additional space, equipment and a carer which is not possible within the space of a standard accessible toilet (Changing Places Consortium 2015). All new buildings and major refurbishments should provide a CP toilet i.e., bench and hoist to allow changing of pads for someone with (e.g.) paraplegia. Consideration should be made to such provision in even minor refurbishments, particularly if they include the installation of accessible toilets. Preference should be given to one CP toilet over two accessible toilets. A CP toilet is usually 12m2 and must include: • height-adjustable, adult-sized changing bench • ceiling track hoist system • adequate space for the disabled person and up to two assistants • peninsular toilet with space both sides for assistants • privacy screen • wide paper roll • large waste disposal bin • washbasin, preferably height adjustable • Back rest on toilet seat • Showers are recommended but not required (Changing Places Consortium 2015). Page 25 of 31 FIGURE 4 Example design: BS8300 Changing Places facility (Changing Places Consortium pg. 32 2015) Plan view Page 26 of 31 Figure 5 Recommended heights for fittings (Changing Places Consortium page 35 2015) Elevation view Elevation view Page 27 of 31 4 How these guidelines were created

### 4.1 Mission
To remove the barriers to accessing life, so people can express their brilliance.

### 4.2 Our paradigms
We genuinely believe that anyone can work in science. We believe that having a diverse workforce enhances the quality and utility of the science created.

### 4.3 Key definitions
The core workplace of science is the laboratory. In these guidelines “Labs" refers to laboratories, manufacturing and production lines, engineering facilities, etc. “Scientists” refers to scientists, technologists, engineers, mathematicians, and healthcare professionals etc. “Disabled” relates to people who are disabled, D/deaf, or have long term health conditions (both physical and mental), illnesses, or injuries, which have a significant impact on their ability to carry out everyday tasks.

### 4.4 Aim
The aim was to create a set of documents that would provide a pragmatic and useful guide on to how to create an accessible lab workplace. We wished to accumulate relevant guidelines for lab contexts, edit them for relevancy, expand them in order to be as comprehensive as possible, and share them with the scientific community. The guidelines are mostly created from previously published work, which we cite. We wanted to provide guidelines for the whole of the lab work ecosystem, and to consider all types of impairments and disabilities. • Structural access – physical design of laboratory and fixed equipment (e.g., hoods, sinks etc.) • Equipment access – design and use of movable equipment (e.g., microscopes, centrifuges, PCR machines etc.) • Protocol access – adaptation of lab protocols to accommodate access needs (e.g., seated working, evacuation protocols, lone working etc.) • Dissemination access – work done in laboratories must be shared with the wider world. Access issues can be encountered in consultation and dissemination events, meetings, conferences, the publication of work on web pages and in journal articles. • General working practices access – adaptation of usual HR and working practices (e.g., part time or flexible hours), assisting disabled staff to access to relevant benefits, accessible transport, and parking etc.

### 4.5 Team expertise
A significant proportion of the Access All Areas in Labs team have disabilities themselves, with lived experience of impairments in mobility, vision, stamina, dexterity, mental wellbeing, cognitive focus, and a range of neurodiversities. They have worked in microbiological, immunological, engineering, Page 28 of 31 electronic, clinical trial, and pharmacy settings as students, researchers, principal investigators, technicians, and administrators.

### 4.6 Methods
We searched scientific databases (MEDLINE, EMBASE); grey literature; professional magazines; online resources; relevant charities and trade unions; centres for disability studies; consultants that support disabled researchers and employers. We snowballed contacts and resources from the originally identified literature. We also conducted a survey of people with an interest in lab access about barriers and solutions to lab access (Deane 2023c) along with a set of case study interviews examining solutions to lab access (AAAiLabs 2023). We identified a key guideline or two at the start of the creation of each of our guidelines. This would then be combined with information from other guidelines, data from the survey and case studies, and combined with the team’s lived expertise to allow us to provide comprehensive guidelines with exemplars of implementation solutions across a range of settings and impairments.

### 4.7 Amendments

sections.content: Page 1 of 18 Purpose of Guidelines These guidelines focus on the key accessibility considerations when designing and specifying equipment for laboratory spaces. sections.heading: 1.1 Seven Principles of Universal Design
sections.content: The seven Principles of Universal Design (National Disability Authority 2012) were developed to guide the design of environments, products, and communications.

blocks.text: The seven Principles of Universal Design (National Disability Authority 2012) were developed to guide the design of environments, products, and communications.

sections.heading: 1.1.1 Principle 1: Equitable Use The design should be useful and marketable to people with diverse abilities. Guidelines:
sections.content: • Provide the same means of use for all users: identical whenever possible; equivalent when not. • Avoid segregating or stigmatizing any users. • Provisions for privacy, security, and safety should be equally available to all users. • Make the design appealing to all users. • Ensure dignity in use for all users.

sections.heading: 1.1.2 Principle 2: Flexibility in Use The design should accommodate a wide range of individual preferences and abilities. Guidelines:
sections.content: • Provide choice in methods of use. • Accommodate right- or left-handed access and use. • Facilitate the user's accuracy and precision. • Provide adaptability to the user's pace.

sections.heading: 1.1.3 Principle 3: Simple and Intuitive Use Use of the design should be easy to understand, regardless of the user's experience, knowledge, language skills, or current concentration level. Guidelines:
sections.content: • Eliminate unnecessary complexity. • Be consistent with user expectations and intuition. • Accommodate a wide range of literacy and language skills. • Arrange information consistent with its importance. • Provide effective prompting and feedback during and after task completion.

sections.heading: 1.1.4 Principle 4: Perceptible Information The design should communicate necessary information effectively to the user, regardless of ambient conditions or the user's sensory abilities. Guidelines:
sections.content: • Use different modes (pictorial, verbal, tactile) for redundant presentation of essential information. • Provide adequate contrast between essential information and its surroundings. • Maximize "legibility" of essential information. • Differentiate elements in ways that can be described (i.e., make it easy to give instructions or directions). Page 7 of 18 • Provide compatibility with a variety of techniques or devices used by people with sensory limitations.

sections.heading: 1.1.5 Principle 5: Tolerance for Error The design should minimise hazards and the adverse consequences of accidental or unintended actions. Guidelines:
sections.content: • Arrange elements to minimize hazards and errors: most used elements, most accessible; hazardous elements eliminated, isolated, or shielded. • Provide warnings of hazards and errors. • Provide fail safe features. • Discourage unconscious action in tasks that require vigilance.

sections.heading: 1.1.6 Principle 6: Low Physical Effort The design should be sufficient such that it can be used efficiently and comfortably and with a minimum of fatigue. Guidelines:
sections.content: • Allow user to maintain a neutral body position. • Use reasonable operating forces. • Minimize repetitive actions. • Minimize sustained physical effort. 1.1.7 Principle 7: Size and Space for Approach and Use Appropriate size and space must be provided for approach, reach, manipulation, and use regardless of user's body size, posture, or mobility. Guidelines: • Provide a clear line of sight to important elements for any seated or standing user. • Make reach to all components comfortable for any seated or standing user. • Accommodate variations in hand and grip size. • Provide adequate space for the use of assistive devices or personal assistance.

sections.heading: 1.2 The social model of disability
sections.content: These guidelines are informed by the Social Model of Disability (Oliver 1990; Scope n.d.). This proposes that the majority of disability is caused by a lack of accommodation for impairments and differences. For example, a wheelchair user cannot get into a building because there are steps before the entrance. This is disabling not because the person is using a wheelchair but due to a lack of provision of a ramp. The responsibility for access lies with the owners of the building, not with the disabled person. “Barriers can make it impossible or very difficult to access jobs, buildings or services, but the biggest barrier of all is the problem of people’s attitude to disability. Removing the barriers is the best way to include millions of disabled people in our society” (TUC 2019).

sections.heading: 1.4 The benefits of accessible labs
sections.content: Labs are often designed without consideration to disability access due to the historic assumption that disabled scientists could not work safely in such environments. If disabled people’s needs are not designed into work and workplaces, then few disabled people will be able to work there. This is part of why there is a significant under representation of disabled people working in science, technology, engineering, and maths (STEM). Whilst approximately 22% of the UK adult population of working age are disabled, only around 3.8% of UK STEM academics are identified as disabled (Joice 2021). The lack of diversity in research participants and scientists is a factor in wasteful research due to serious flaws in prioritisation, design, sampling, analysis and interpretation, etc. (Glasziou 2018; Macleod 2014; JLA 2023). Research that is informed by a diverse multidisciplinary team is better able to ensure practicality, utility, and impact (Deane 2014 and 2019, Schroeder 2022). The opportunity cost of not having disabled scientists with their diversity of experience and expertise is likely to be significant. Additionally, most disabilities are acquired; the loss of highly qualified scientists from the field when they acquire a disability is a substantial loss on the investment in their training. We start with the assumption that all disabled scientists are able to work in labs, if the labs are designed with their access needs met. Safety issues can be designed “out” of the labs; either in the structural or equipment design or in the protocols used. Accessibility also includes the design of the work processes, staff knowledge and attitudes. Accessible labs will allow a greater proportion of disabled scientists to be trained and work in lab settings in a safe and comfortable manner. We genuinely believe this improved diversity in the workforce will enhance the quality and potential profitability of the work done in laboratory settings. Page 9 of 18

sections.content: There are detailed specifications below, but the key access considerations and solutions can be summarised as follows.

sections.heading: 2.1 Acceptability for the whole team
sections.content: • All access solutions should be considered with regard to their impact on the work of the whole team. There is the potential for clashes between ergonomic needs and/or access needs. Perfect solutions for one access need may create barriers for another. Consultations should take place to ensure the removal of all absolute access barriers and the identification of acceptable compromises.

sections.heading: 2.2 Mobility
sections.content: • Wheelchair users need to be able to operate the equipment from a sitting position. • Electric wheelchairs in particular have the capacity to damage equipment by knocking into it. Consideration should be given to the robustness and positioning of the equipment in the laboratory.

sections.heading: 2.4 Sensory
sections.content: • Good colour contrast, matt surfaces. • Particular care should be taken to choice of colours and colour blindness • Consideration should be given to tactile differences for buttons / handles. • Good lighting. • Signs and alarms should have two modes e.g., audible and visual fire alarms, visual and tactile signs. • Equipment should run as silently as possible. sections.heading: 3.1 Visual Access: Colours
sections.content: Contrasting colours should be used to distinguish once thing from another; a difference of at least 30 points in light reflectance value (BS8300-2, 2018). Handles should be a different colour from doors. Switches should be a contrasting colour compared to the surround.

sections.heading: 3.2 Visual Access: Lighting
sections.content: Where a piece of equipment provides lighting onto a specific area flexible lighting options should be provided with a view to light intensity and possibly spectrum. Lighting must be sufficient and not create glare. Where flat screen controls are used, lighting levels and contrast of the screens should be adjustable. Consideration should be given to lighting reflections on flat screens when viewed from sitting and standing positions.

sections.heading: 3.3 Hearing Access: Acoustic adjustments
sections.content: Consideration should be given to the background noise level of equipment e.g., ventilation, hoods, alarms etc. (BS8233 2014) Consideration should be given to the use of sound insulation in equipment to reduce external noise when running. Alarms should include a visual alarm (flashing light) in addition of the auditory alarm. • Consideration should be given to linking auditory information to external equipment e.g., alarms linked to mobile phone apps.

sections.heading: 3.4 Doors
sections.content: All doors on equipment need to be easy to open. They must be light i.e., <30N force to open (Building Regulations 2010). Consideration should be given to powering heavy doors e.g., doors to water jacketed incubators. All lever and pull handles should be easy to grip and use. Some idea of suitable dimensions and clearances can be found in BS8300-2 section 8.4 (2018). Door handles should be of a contrasting colour to the door. Consideration should be given to a contrasting texture. All door locks should use large levers that can be operated easily e.g., with a closed fist.

sections.heading: 3.6 Services and controls
sections.content: Control panels fascia should be of a contrasting colour to the rest of the equipment or be outlined with a contrasting colour paint line (a difference of at least 30 points in light reflectance value, BS8300-2 (2018)). Switches should be a contrasting colour to the fascia. Consideration should be given to the location of switches and control panels. Ideally, they will be reachable from a wheelchair or by someone of restricted growth, and not require reaching above shoulder height. They should not require reaching over hot plates, water baths etc. Equipment controls should: • have with clearly defined controls (contrasting colours and/or tactile difference) • controls that do not require strength or dexterity to operate • controls that can be seen and used from a seated and standing position. Consideration should be given to location, height, and lighting levels. Consideration should be given to controls that can be linked to external access solutions e.g., large touch screens, voice activated controls etc. Consideration to be given to provision of equipment that gives audible speech output of the functions chosen. Where possible control labels should use both words and symbols – particularly where they indicate hazards. Control labels should use sans serif font of a suitable size. There should be clear contrast between background and text with coloured backgrounds preferred. To assist wheelchair users who have reduced range of reach, services and controls should comply with all of the following. Consumer units should be mounted so that the switches are between 1350mm and 1450mm above floor level. (Building Regulations 2010) Switches, sockets, stopcocks and controls, are located with their centre line 700-1000mm above floor level and a minimum of 700mm (measured horizontally) from an inside corner and are not positioned behind appliances. (Building Regulations 2010) Power isolators should be located within the same height range. (Building Regulations 2010) To assist people who rely on technological solutions to interact with their environment, services and controls should comply with all of the following, where relevant: Page 13 of 18 • Equipment should allow connectivity with other equipment to allow the display of data and/or allow networked control of the equipment e.g., alarms that signal mobile phone apps that vibrate, or voice activated control systems. • It is highly likely that some level of customisation will be required to successfully interface accessibility technology with laboratory equipment. To make this as easy as possible, equipment should ideally conform to open standards for interface and control, or if not the interface (hardware and software) should be sufficiently documented by the manufacturer. • Where custom hardware or software needs to be produced in order to interface between accessibility aids and laboratory equipment then consideration should be given to investigating if there is a pre-existing solution that could be adapted. Use an open-source solution if there is a suitable one available, if one needs to be created it should be open source. • The current move towards lab automation generally improves accessibility by removing the need to interact physically with laboratory equipment. However, the method of control of this equipment needs to be accessible. • Maintenance or upgrades of laboratory equipment should consider accessibility solutions that have already been implemented and should maintain functionality.

Consideration to be given to provision of equipment that gives audible speech output of the functions chosen.
Where possible control labels should use both words and symbols – particularly where they indicate hazards.
Control labels should use sans serif font of a suitable size. There should be clear contrast between background and text with coloured backgrounds preferred.
To assist wheelchair users who have reduced range of reach, services and controls should comply with all of the following.
Consumer units should be mounted so that the switches are between 1350mm and 1450mm above floor level. (Building Regulations 2010)

Switches, sockets, stopcocks and controls, are located with their centre line 700-1000mm above floor level and a minimum of 700mm (measured horizontally) from an inside corner and are not positioned behind appliances. (Building Regulations 2010)
Power isolators should be located within the same height range. (Building Regulations 2010)
To assist people who rely on technological solutions to interact with their environment, services and controls should comply with all of the following, where relevant:
Page 13 of 18

Equipment should allow connectivity with other equipment to allow the display of data and/or allow networked control of the equipment e.g., alarms that signal mobile phone apps that vibrate, or voice activated control systems. • It is highly likely that some level of customisation will be required to successfully interface accessibility technology with laboratory equipment. To make this as easy as possible, equipment should ideally conform to open standards for interface and control, or if not the interface (hardware and software) should be sufficiently documented by the manufacturer. • Where custom hardware or software needs to be produced in order to interface between accessibility aids and laboratory equipment then consideration should be given to investigating if there is a pre-existing solution that could be adapted. Use an open-source solution if there is a suitable one available, if one needs to be created it should be open source. • The current move towards lab automation generally improves accessibility by removing the need to interact physically with laboratory equipment. However, the method of control of this equipment needs to be accessible. • Maintenance or upgrades of laboratory equipment should consider accessibility solutions that have already been implemented and should maintain functionality.

sections.heading: 3.7 Cleaning and decontamination
sections.content: Equipment should not require much strength, dexterity, or co-ordination in order to dismantle it for standard cleaning or decontamination protocols. Reassembly should be clearly successful (e.g., click lock) and fail safe, with a single (correct) way for components to fit together.

Reassembly should be clearly successful (e.g., click lock) and fail safe, with a single (correct) way for components to fit together.

sections.heading: 3.8 Documentation
sections.content: All aids and adaptations should be properly documented. Manuals, risk assessments, SOPs, etc should be generated or obtained and kept.

sections.heading: 3.9 Design consultation
sections.content: When designing equipment, best practice is to consult with a panel of users who include those with a range of impairments. In particular those with sensory, mobility, strength, and dexterity impairments. Page 14 of 18

sections.heading: 4.1 Mission
sections.content: To remove the barriers to accessing life, so people can express their brilliance.

sections.heading: 4.2 Our paradigms
sections.content: We genuinely believe that anyone can work in science. We believe that having a diverse workforce enhances the quality and utility of the science created.

sections.heading: 4.3 Key definitions
sections.content: The core workplace of science is the laboratory. In these guidelines “Labs" refers to laboratories, manufacturing and production lines, engineering facilities, etc. “Scientists” refers to scientists, technologists, engineers, mathematicians, and healthcare professionals etc. “Disabled” relates to people who are disabled, D/deaf, or have long term health conditions (both physical and mental), illnesses, or injuries, which have a significant impact on their ability to carry out everyday tasks.

“Scientists” refers to scientists, technologists, engineers, mathematicians, and healthcare professionals etc.

“Disabled” relates to people who are disabled, D/deaf, or have long term health conditions (both physical and mental), illnesses, or injuries, which have a significant impact on their ability to carry out everyday tasks.

sections.heading: 4.4 Aim
sections.content: The aim was to create a set of documents that would provide a pragmatic and useful guide on to how to create an accessible lab workplace. We wished to accumulate relevant guidelines for lab contexts, edit them for relevancy, expand them in order to be as comprehensive as possible, and share them with the scientific community. The guidelines are mostly created from previously published work, which we cite. We wanted to provide guidelines for the whole of the lab work ecosystem, and to consider all types of impairments and disabilities. • Structural access – physical design of laboratory and fixed equipment (e.g., hoods, sinks etc.) • Equipment access – design and use of movable equipment (e.g., microscopes, centrifuges, PCR machines etc.) • Protocol access – adaptation of lab protocols to accommodate access needs (e.g., seated working, evacuation protocols, lone working etc.) • Dissemination access – work done in laboratories must be shared with the wider world. Access issues can be encountered in consultation and dissemination events, meetings, conferences, the publication of work on web pages and in journal articles. • General working practices access – adaptation of usual HR and working practices (e.g., part time or flexible hours), assisting disabled staff to access to relevant benefits, accessible transport, and parking etc.

sections.heading: 4.6 Methods
sections.content: We searched scientific databases (MEDLINE, EMBASE); grey literature; professional magazines; online resources; relevant charities and trade unions; centres for disability studies; consultants that support disabled researchers and employers. We snowballed contacts and resources from the originally identified literature. We also conducted a survey of people with an interest in lab access about barriers and solutions to lab access (Deane 2023) along with a set of case study interviews examining solutions to lab access (AAAiLabs 2023). We identified a key guideline or two at the start of the creation of each of our guidelines. This would then be combined with information from other guidelines, data from the survey and case studies, and combined with the team’s lived expertise to allow us to provide comprehensive guidelines with exemplars of implementation solutions across a range of settings and impairments.

Disclaimer These guidelines are provided in good faith and are intended as an aid to good practice in accessibility. They cannot replace sound judgement, professional care, or common sense. They should be read and applied in conjunction with appropriate standards, and all relevant local regulations, codes of practice, and laws. These guidelines constitute a live document and may be subject to change in the future where the authors consider it appropriate in the light of new information or developments in the field of accessibility. Comments and Corrections We welcome comments and corrections on these guidelines that will allow us to enhance the next version’s quality and relevancy. If you have suggestions for changes, please email Dr Katherine Deane k.deane@uea.ac.uk Acknowledgements These guidelines were created by the Access All Areas in Labs team which included: • Katherine Deane, Associate Professor and Access Ambassador, University of East Anglia, k.deane@uea.ac.uk • Thomas Fadden, Purple Reach Disability Access Consultancy, tom@purplereach.co.uk • Jenny Camaradou, Independent Expert on Knowledge Exchange, Grant Writing, and Patient Engagement, jenny@healthclusternet.eu • Peter Hemmins, Senior Lab Technician, Productivity East, Science Faculty University of East Anglia • Dan Burrill, Lab Technician, Science Faculty, University of East Anglia Funding This project was funded by a grant award from Innovate UK to the Cell & Gene Therapy Catapult. Additionally Katherine Deane, UEA, is supported by the National Institute for Health and Care Research (NIHR) Applied Research Collaboration East of England (NIHR ARC EoE) at Cambridge and Peterborough NHS Foundation Trust. The views expressed are those Page 2 of 18 of the author[s] and not necessarily those of the NIHR or the Department of Health and Social Care. About the Cell and Gene Therapy Catapult: The Cell and Gene Therapy Catapult is an independent innovation and technology organisation committed to the advancement of cell and gene therapies with a vision of a thriving industry delivering life changing advanced therapies to the world. Its aim is to create powerful collaborations which overcome challenges to the advancement of the sector. With over 400 experts covering all aspects of advanced therapies, it applies its unique capabilities and assets, collaborates with academia, industry and healthcare providers to develop new technology and innovation. Disability Authority 2012) were developed to guide the design of environments, products, and communications. • Provide the same means of use for all users: identical whenever possible; equivalent when not. • Avoid segregating or stigmatizing any users. • Provisions for privacy, security, and safety should be equally available to all users. • Make the design appealing to all users. • Ensure dignity in use for all users. • Provide choice in methods of use. • Accommodate right- or left-handed access and use. • Facilitate the user's accuracy and precision. • Provide adaptability to the user's pace. • Eliminate unnecessary complexity. • Be consistent with user expectations and intuition. • Accommodate a wide range of literacy and language skills. • Arrange information consistent with its importance. • Provide effective prompting and feedback during and after task completion. • Use different modes (pictorial, verbal, tactile) for redundant presentation of essential information. • Provide adequate contrast between essential information and its surroundings. • Maximize "legibility" of essential information. • Differentiate elements in ways that can be described (i.e., make it easy to give instructions or directions). Page 7 of 18 • Provide compatibility with a variety of techniques or devices used by people with sensory limitations. • Arrange elements to minimize hazards and errors: most used elements, most accessible; hazardous elements eliminated, isolated, or shielded. • Provide warnings of hazards and errors. • Provide fail safe features. • Discourage unconscious action in tasks that require vigilance. • Allow user to maintain a neutral body position. • Use reasonable operating forces. • Minimize repetitive actions. • Minimize sustained physical effort. 1.1.7 Principle 7: Size and Space for Approach and Use Appropriate size and space must be provided for approach, reach, manipulation, and use regardless of user's body size, posture, or mobility. Guidelines: • Provide a clear line of sight to important elements for any seated or standing user. • Make reach to all components comfortable for any seated or standing user. • Accommodate variations in hand and grip size. • Provide adequate space for the use of assistive devices or personal assistance. These guidelines are informed by the Social Model of Disability (Oliver 1990; Scope n.d.). This proposes that the majority of disability is caused by a lack of accommodation for impairments and differences. For example, a wheelchair user cannot get into a building because there are steps before the entrance. This is disabling not because the person is using a wheelchair but due to a lack of provision of a ramp. The responsibility for access lies with the owners of the building, not with the disabled person. “Barriers can make it impossible or very difficult to access jobs, buildings or services, but the biggest barrier of all is the problem of people’s attitude to disability. Removing the barriers is the best way to include millions of disabled people in our society” (TUC 2019). Page 8 of 18 All employers have a legal duty under the Equality Act 2010 to proactively make reasonable adjustments to remove, reduce or prevent any disadvantages that disabled workers face (TUC 2019). In order to achieve equity for disabled people, work may need to be organised differently, support provided, and barriers removed. Labs are often designed without consideration to disability access due to the historic assumption that disabled scientists could not work safely in such environments. If disabled people’s needs are not designed into work and workplaces, then few disabled people will be able to work there. This is part of why there is a significant under representation of disabled people working in science, technology, engineering, and maths (STEM). Whilst approximately 22% of the UK adult population of working age are disabled, only around 3.8% of UK STEM academics are identified as disabled (Joice 2021). The lack of diversity in research participants and scientists is a factor in wasteful research due to serious flaws in prioritisation, design, sampling, analysis and interpretation, etc. (Glasziou 2018; Macleod 2014; JLA 2023). Research that is informed by a diverse multidisciplinary team is better able to ensure practicality, utility, and impact (Deane 2014 and 2019, Schroeder 2022). The opportunity cost of not having disabled scientists with their diversity of experience and expertise is likely to be significant. Additionally, most disabilities are acquired; the loss of highly qualified scientists from the field when they acquire a disability is a substantial loss on the investment in their training. We start with the assumption that all disabled scientists are able to work in labs, if the labs are designed with their access needs met. Safety issues can be designed “out” of the labs; either in the structural or equipment design or in the protocols used. Accessibility also includes the design of the work processes, staff knowledge and attitudes. Accessible labs will allow a greater proportion of disabled scientists to be trained and work in lab settings in a safe and comfortable manner. We genuinely believe this improved diversity in the workforce will enhance the quality and potential profitability of the work done in laboratory settings. Page 9 of 18 There are detailed specifications below, but the key access considerations and solutions can be summarised as follows. • All access solutions should be considered with regard to their impact on the work of the whole team. There is the potential for clashes between ergonomic needs and/or access needs. Perfect solutions for one access need may create barriers for another. Consultations should take place to ensure the removal of all absolute access barriers and the identification of acceptable compromises. • Wheelchair users need to be able to operate the equipment from a sitting position. • Electric wheelchairs in particular have the capacity to damage equipment by knocking into it. Consideration should be given to the robustness and positioning of the equipment in the laboratory. • All taps should be lever type. • All doors should be light. • Door handles and locks should allow easy grip and have good colour contrast • Buttons should have good clearance around them (to allow for lack of accuracy) • Good colour contrast, matt surfaces. • Particular care should be taken to choice of colours and colour blindness • Consideration should be given to tactile differences for buttons / handles. • Good lighting. • Signs and alarms should have two modes e.g., audible and visual fire alarms, visual and tactile signs. • Equipment should run as silently as possible. Consideration should be given to the quality of the auditory environment, noise of fans etc can be either distracting or reduce ease of spoken communication. • Flat screens should have adjustable lighting levels, good colour contrast, good choice of colours. Text should be large and ideally adjustable in terms of size and contrast with background. • Equipment controls and monitoring should be able to be linked to other access equipment e.g., voice activated controls. Use of open standards is highly preferred where these exist, in their absence any protocol for interfacing with Page 10 of 18 equipment should be well documented and not rely on proprietary hardware or software. ### 4.6 Methods ......................................................................................................................... 16 4.7 Amendments .................................................................................................................. 16

### 1.1 Seven Principles of Universal Design
The seven Principles of Universal Design (National Disability Authority 2012) were developed to guide the design of environments, products, and communications.

#### 1.1.1 Principle 1: Equitable Use The design should be useful and marketable to people with diverse abilities. Guidelines:
• Provide the same means of use for all users: identical whenever possible; equivalent when not. • Avoid segregating or stigmatizing any users. • Provisions for privacy, security, and safety should be equally available to all users. • Make the design appealing to all users. • Ensure dignity in use for all users.

#### 1.1.2 Principle 2: Flexibility in Use The design should accommodate a wide range of individual preferences and abilities. Guidelines:
• Provide choice in methods of use. • Accommodate right- or left-handed access and use. • Facilitate the user's accuracy and precision. • Provide adaptability to the user's pace.

#### 1.1.3 Principle 3: Simple and Intuitive Use Use of the design should be easy to understand, regardless of the user's experience, knowledge, language skills, or current concentration level. Guidelines:
• Eliminate unnecessary complexity. • Be consistent with user expectations and intuition. • Accommodate a wide range of literacy and language skills. • Arrange information consistent with its importance. • Provide effective prompting and feedback during and after task completion.

#### 1.1.4 Principle 4: Perceptible Information The design should communicate necessary information effectively to the user, regardless of ambient conditions or the user's sensory abilities. Guidelines:
• Use different modes (pictorial, verbal, tactile) for redundant presentation of essential information. • Provide adequate contrast between essential information and its surroundings. • Maximize "legibility" of essential information. • Differentiate elements in ways that can be described (i.e., make it easy to give instructions or directions). Page 7 of 18 • Provide compatibility with a variety of techniques or devices used by people with sensory limitations.

#### 1.1.5 Principle 5: Tolerance for Error The design should minimise hazards and the adverse consequences of accidental or unintended actions. Guidelines:
• Arrange elements to minimize hazards and errors: most used elements, most accessible; hazardous elements eliminated, isolated, or shielded. • Provide warnings of hazards and errors. • Provide fail safe features. • Discourage unconscious action in tasks that require vigilance.

#### 1.1.6 Principle 6: Low Physical Effort The design should be sufficient such that it can be used efficiently and comfortably and with a minimum of fatigue. Guidelines:
• Allow user to maintain a neutral body position. • Use reasonable operating forces. • Minimize repetitive actions. • Minimize sustained physical effort. 1.1.7 Principle 7: Size and Space for Approach and Use Appropriate size and space must be provided for approach, reach, manipulation, and use regardless of user's body size, posture, or mobility. Guidelines: • Provide a clear line of sight to important elements for any seated or standing user. • Make reach to all components comfortable for any seated or standing user. • Accommodate variations in hand and grip size. • Provide adequate space for the use of assistive devices or personal assistance.

### 1.2 The social model of disability
These guidelines are informed by the Social Model of Disability (Oliver 1990; Scope n.d.). This proposes that the majority of disability is caused by a lack of accommodation for impairments and differences. For example, a wheelchair user cannot get into a building because there are steps before the entrance. This is disabling not because the person is using a wheelchair but due to a lack of provision of a ramp. The responsibility for access lies with the owners of the building, not with the disabled person. “Barriers can make it impossible or very difficult to access jobs, buildings or services, but the biggest barrier of all is the problem of people’s attitude to disability. Removing the barriers is the best way to include millions of disabled people in our society” (TUC 2019).

### 1.3 The duty to make reasonable adjustments
Page 8 of 18 All employers have a legal duty under the Equality Act 2010 to proactively make reasonable adjustments to remove, reduce or prevent any disadvantages that disabled workers face (TUC 2019). In order to achieve equity for disabled people, work may need to be organised differently, support provided, and barriers removed.

### 1.4 The benefits of accessible labs
Labs are often designed without consideration to disability access due to the historic assumption that disabled scientists could not work safely in such environments. If disabled people’s needs are not designed into work and workplaces, then few disabled people will be able to work there. This is part of why there is a significant under representation of disabled people working in science, technology, engineering, and maths (STEM). Whilst approximately 22% of the UK adult population of working age are disabled, only around 3.8% of UK STEM academics are identified as disabled (Joice 2021). The lack of diversity in research participants and scientists is a factor in wasteful research due to serious flaws in prioritisation, design, sampling, analysis and interpretation, etc. (Glasziou 2018; Macleod 2014; JLA 2023). Research that is informed by a diverse multidisciplinary team is better able to ensure practicality, utility, and impact (Deane 2014 and 2019, Schroeder 2022). The opportunity cost of not having disabled scientists with their diversity of experience and expertise is likely to be significant. Additionally, most disabilities are acquired; the loss of highly qualified scientists from the field when they acquire a disability is a substantial loss on the investment in their training. We start with the assumption that all disabled scientists are able to work in labs, if the labs are designed with their access needs met. Safety issues can be designed “out” of the labs; either in the structural or equipment design or in the protocols used. Accessibility also includes the design of the work processes, staff knowledge and attitudes. Accessible labs will allow a greater proportion of disabled scientists to be trained and work in lab settings in a safe and comfortable manner. We genuinely believe this improved diversity in the workforce will enhance the quality and potential profitability of the work done in laboratory settings. Page 9 of 18

## 2 Key Access Considerations
There are detailed specifications below, but the key access considerations and solutions can be summarised as follows.

### 2.1 Acceptability for the whole team
• All access solutions should be considered with regard to their impact on the work of the whole team. There is the potential for clashes between ergonomic needs and/or access needs. Perfect solutions for one access need may create barriers for another. Consultations should take place to ensure the removal of all absolute access barriers and the identification of acceptable compromises.

### 2.2 Mobility
• Wheelchair users need to be able to operate the equipment from a sitting position. • Electric wheelchairs in particular have the capacity to damage equipment by knocking into it. Consideration should be given to the robustness and positioning of the equipment in the laboratory.

### 2.3 Dexterity and strength

### 2.4 Sensory

Consideration should be given to the quality of the auditory environment, noise of fans etc can be either distracting or reduce ease of spoken communication. • Flat screens should have adjustable lighting levels, good colour contrast, good choice of colours. Text should be large and ideally adjustable in terms of size and contrast with background.
