For example, the alarm sounds at reception during office hours, Page 12 of 30 but is diverted to security out of hours. Both the reception and security teams are aware of how to override the door lock, and to sensitively respond to someone in distress. Tests should be run at least twice annually to check that the alarm works and that it is responded to promptly. There should be a clear communication strategy to ensure that users are informed when access features are out of use e.g., lifts, accessible toilets. For example, emails and/or text alerts to all workers with a personal emergency evacuation plan due to their mobility impairments informing them when a lift is out of order. When considering the information to be relayed consideration should be given to providing: • Information on the piece of equipment that is out of order • Its location • The time/date it went out of order • The expected time/date that it is hoped to be repaired by • Contact details for any queries • Alternate equipment or routes that can be used in the meantime – with location and possibly maps The communication plan should include options to send another message to appropriate disabled staff once the facility is back in working order, or if the repair is delayed. Consideration must be given to ensuring the format is accessible for everyone receiving the messages. The Access All Areas in Labs Dissemination Access Guideline (2023) provides detailed information on how to do this. • Example: Voice messages may be left for someone with dyslexia in preference to (or in addition to) e-mail messages. Policies should escalate the priority of the repair if it is not achieved within a previously agreed timeframe e.g., within two working days for the repair of an accessible toilet. Records should be kept allowing tracking of time out of action for access facilities so as to identify if this is likely to have had negative impact on disabled staff’s ability to work well or access certain facilities. A reasonable accommodation would be to record any impact of these facility breakdowns so that they can be taken into account when conducting an appraisal of a disabled employee’s work, or when organising alternate work practices e.g., working from home. • Example: A disabled employee uses a wheelchair for mobility. Their lab is on the second floor. There are two lifts, one at each end of a long building, and the accessible toilet is on the ground floor. The lift that is closest to the disabled employee’s lab and the accessible toilet downstairs is frequently broken for days or weeks on end. This means that the employee is regularly having to take long breaks in order to use the far lift to reach the accessible toilet. He raises this in his Page 13 of 30 performance review, and it is agreed that the impact of this extra travel time will be taken into account when assessing his efficiency. A query is also raised with Estates regarding what plans are in place to permanently resolve the lift’s reliability. • Example: It is agreed that an employee with poor mobility who works on the third floor, can work from home on days where planned maintenance of the lift is scheduled. If the lift goes out of order, Estates send out a message to their “high priority lift list” to let them know how long the repair is likely to take. If it is predicted to take more than half a day, it has been agreed that the employee can leave early and work from home until the lift is repaired. Particular care should be paid to the cleanliness of accessible facilities. Staff that use them often have no other option but to continue to use them even if they find them in an unclean state. • Example: After complaints from a wheelchair user about the lift smelling of rotting garbage, the cleaning team add a sanitising step to clean the lift after it has been used to remove garbage bags from upper floors. Unfortunately, the extra space that is provided in accessible facilities can be viewed as storage space by staff unaware that the space is essential to allow wheelchairs to turn, or to have space for the assistance of carers. It is not uncommon for disabled staff to find spare chairs, coat racks, mops, buckets etc. stored in accessible toilets. Cleaning staff are particularly important in checking on the appropriate use of the facilities, as they should be checking on the cleanliness of these at regular intervals (just as they do for the standard toilet facilities). The cleaning teams should be empowered to remove anything inappropriately stored in toilets and let the building manager know of the issue. It can be challenging to ensure access is retained whilst building works are ongoing. Consideration should be given to whether key routes (e.g., step free) will be blocked, or key facilities (e.g., lifts) will be put out of action during the works. Staff should be consulted to identify alternate routes or facilities well in advance of the works starting. Clear signage should give notice of the works planned and identify the person to be contacted in the event of queries. Disabled staff who cannot access a certain area of a building or facility that is essential for the conduct of their role, should have their work re-evaluated and adjusted to accommodate this temporary lack of access e.g., changed to work from home, certain tasks handed over to others in the team etc. All workers conducting the building works (including contractors) should be aware of the primacy of ensuring ongoing access. • Example: All contractors are required to sign an agreement emphasising that inappropriate use of accessible parking bays is always unacceptable. Security is Page 14 of 30 aware that anyone inappropriately using an accessible parking bay should be given a parking fine, and that if it is a contractor’s vehicle, they should contact Estates who will follow up with a formal complaint to the company in addition to the fine. • Example: Skips for building rubble are required. The works will block one building entrance and the skips will be placed over three accessible parking bays associated with this entrance. Three additional accessible parking bays will be marked out next to the alternate entrance to the building for the duration of the works. • Example: Senior staff are usually the only staff provided with parking spaces on site. A disabled worker with mobility impairments may be provided with a designated parking space close to the building irrespective of their seniority. If they use a wheelchair or other mobility equipment, then a larger accessible parking bay should be provided. The Structural Access Guideline (Deane 2023a) provides detailed descriptions of signage for navigation and identification of accessible facilities and equipment (e.g., lifts, hearing loops). The Dissemination Access Guideline (Deane 2023c) provides detailed descriptions of what information is need and how to provide information on documents and web pages in accessible formats. In particular we recommend providing access information on a dedicated webpage that is easy to find from the front page of the company’s or venue’s website. There really is no such thing as “too much” access information. • Example: Accessible toilet information on a company’s web page includes: o A map of the location o Photos to aid identification of location and content of toilet facilities o Dimensions of the toilet, including which side the transfer is on o Contact details for any concerns regarding cleaning or maintenance. If rooms, facilities or equipment can be booked by staff then access information should be provided in the booking form e.g., step free venue, availability of hearing loop, ability to book out “easy grip” versions of equipment. It is recommended that booking systems encourage best practice behaviours e.g., allowing the room booking system to select only “fully accessible” rooms e.g., with step free access, with hearing loops and microphones; and that the use of these rooms is a mandatory requirement for public events. An employer might reallocate minor or subsidiary duties to another worker as a disabled worker has difficulty doing them because of his disability (EHRC 2011). Page 15 of 30 • Example: For example, the job involves occasionally going up a set of stairs to access the top of a vat to take samples. The employer transfers this work away from a worker whose disability involves mobility impairment. • Example: A lab technician is tasked to setting up a workstation with relevant solutions so that a disabled worker can just program the assistive robot to run a set of protocols and supervise its conduct. An employer should consider if allowing a disabled person to work flexible hours might mitigate some of their impairment. For example, enabling a worker to have additional breaks to overcome fatigue arising from their disability. It could also include permitting parttime working or different working hours to avoid the need to travel in the rush hour if this creates a problem related to an impairment. A phased return to work with a gradual buildup of hours might also be appropriate in some circumstances (EHRC 2011). • Example: A biomedical lab runs a shift system with staff rotating through “early”, “late”, and “night” shifts for two weeks at a time. A disabled scientist with epilepsy and autism struggles to maintain their medication and sleep routines to a sufficiently stringent standard to prevent fitting. They are allowed to work an “early” shift permanently. This accommodation can be hugely important to allow a disabled worker to optimise the management of their symptoms, particularly fatigue. Travelling in and out of work and moving around a workplace can create excessive fatigue in people with energy limiting conditions (Hale 2021). • Example: An employer relocates the workstation of a newly disabled worker (who now uses a wheelchair) from an inaccessible third floor office to an accessible one on the ground floor. It may be reasonable to move his place of work to other premises of the same employer if the first building is inaccessible (EHRC 2011). • Example: Allowing the worker to work from home for some or all of their role might also be a reasonable adjustment for the employer to make (EHRC 2011). Consideration should be made to ensure online, or hybrid meetings have appropriate access arranged (e.g., sign language interpreters). Hybrid meetings need to be appropriately facilitated to ensure equality of contribution of those online and in person (Dissemination Access Guidelines, Deane 2023c). Page 16 of 30 Absence for rehabilitation, assessment or treatment should not be regarded as the same as standard sick leave. Policies should be in place to identify that this leave is disability-related and comes under specific policies that ensure equity. • Example: An employer allows a person who has become disabled more time off work than would be allowed to non-disabled workers to enable him to have rehabilitation training. A similar adjustment may be appropriate if a disability worsens or if a disabled person needs occasional treatment anyway (EHRC 2011). This could be training in particular pieces of equipment which the disabled person uses, or an alteration to the standard workplace training to reflect the worker’s particular disability (EHRC 2011). Research has identified that employees with protected characteristics are at highest risk of suffering discriminatory or bullying behaviour (Wellcome 2020; Deane 2023d). Therefore, it is strongly recommended that employers provide training aimed at raising awareness and changing the workplace culture e.g., training in preventing disability discrimination and promoting allyship. • Example: All workers are trained in the use of a particular machine, but an employer provides slightly different or longer training for a worker with restricted hand or arm movements (EHRC 2011). • Example: An employer might also provide training in additional software for a visually impaired worker so that he can use a computer with speech output (EHRC 2011). • Example: A disabled employee needs to use an Evacuation Chair in the event of fire. The disabled employee should be given an opportunity to try using the Evacuation Chair with no time pressure. Fire wardens and anyone else who it is reasonable to assume might be required to aid in an evacuation (e.g., security team) should be trained on how to use the chair. Any worker with an impairment that might interfere with their safe evacuation from a building should be provided with a personal emergency evacuation plan (PEEP) (Home Office 2007). This usually includes people with mobility, hearing or visual impairments. However, consideration should be given to other impairments e.g., neurodiversity, where navigation under stress and sensory overload may be problematic. Consideration should be given to additional training needed – both for the disabled member of staff and fire wardens etc. Page 17 of 30 Evacuation protocols may require the disabled worker to carry a mobile phone with them so they can inform security of their location in the event of fire. Some disabled people may only be able to be in a building, or certain areas of a building, when accompanied by another person (who is responsible for assisting their evacuation). It should also be remembered that what a disabled person is prepared to do in exceptional circumstances may differ significantly from what they can reasonably manage in their everyday activities (Home Office 2007). Fire evacuation drills need to balance the relative risks of knowing how to evacuate the building speedily with the risk of the evacuation process itself – especially for workers with mobility impairments. For example, the risk of transferring to an Evacuation Chair from a wheelchair is often not trivial and may risk falls and injuries. Workers who need to use an Evacuation Chair or Powered Stair Climber to aid evacuation from upper floors may be allowed to remain in the stair well for fire drills having contacted security or fire wardens. They would not actually evacuate from the building for the drill. However, the disabled worker should be trained in how to use the Evacuation Chair or Powered Stair Climber (e.g. Super Trac 2021) at another instance. This training should be without time pressure, and with sufficient staff to assist. In the case of an Evacuation Chair the training will aim to ensure the disabled member of staff to learn how to transfer safely from a wheelchair into an Evacuation Chair, and for their assistants (if any) to learn how to safely assist with this. Should a disabled member of staff require assistance to transfer safely then it is likely they will need a safe working protocol that requires them to be accompanied by a suitably trained assistant at all times. In the case of a Powered Stair Climber the disabled person will need to learn how to manoeuvre their wheelchair onto the platform safely. As a Powered Stair Climber does not require a disabled person to transfer out of their wheelchair in order to be evacuated, this option is safer and accommodates a wider range of impairments than an Evacuation Chair. However it is recognised that it does require a staircase with good clearance (1600mm x 1600mm) and is considerably more expensive. Disabled staff who cannot hear fire alarms must have a PEEP created for them. Consideration should be given to the installation of dual alert fire alarm systems (audio and visual alarms). Consideration should be given to the use of a mobile phone app that vibrates in response to alarms. However, this sort of app may be confused by the “process finished” audible alerts from the lab equipment and effectively give false alarms, so this should be tested for utility in the workplace. • Example: A senior manager who is deaf is required to work late and be in the office early on occasion. The office has a 24-hour security presence, and it is necessary for all staff to sign in and out at the security point. An arrangement is made that, should an alarm be raised out of hours when the manager is present, the security guard will contact the manager on their textphone to alert them of the emergency. This was Page 18 of 30 built into the instruction manual on means of escape procedures for all security staff (Home Office 2007). There are a number of potential circumstances in which disabled people may need additional assistance to get themselves and/or their equipment out of the building. For example, an employee becomes unwell and unstable on their feet whilst on the upper floor of a building without a lift or the lift breaks down and a person with limited mobility needs to leave the building from a higher floor. In these cases, it is appropriate to use Evacuation Chairs to help remove the employee safely from the upper floors to the ground floor of the building. Any walking aids should be brought down with them, so they can walk as safely as possible once they reach ground level. Manual wheelchairs are usually light enough to be a single person lift (i.e., less than 25kg). However, they can be an awkward shape so consideration should have been given to the safe removal of a manual wheelchair from a building if the lift is out of action. Another circumstance is that the lift breaks down and an electric wheelchair user needs to leave the building from a higher floor. So obviously you can start by evacuating the disabled person in an Evacuation Chair to the ground floor. It is getting their wheelchair to the ground floor as well that is the challenge. A couple of key facts are important to this example. 1. In a non-emergency evacuation it is essential that a wheelchair user is not left without their wheelchair for an extended period of time. 2. Electric wheelchairs can be large and heavy (commonly between 120-150kg); and the weight is unevenly distributed. It is likely that a plan will have to be created for each wheelchair as they vary substantially in size and weight. Wheelchairs have tie down loops for use in vehicles, so these are likely to be a safe place to affix straps to aid removal of the wheelchair down the stairs. A final circumstance that may need consideration is if an electric wheelchair breaks down on an upper floor. As discussed before an electric wheelchair is essential for the wellbeing of a disabled person and is heavy. Whilst such a chair can be pushed manually to a lift and potentially up a ramp into a taxi or the employee’s wheelchair accessible vehicle; it will be heavy and unwieldy. It should be assumed that a repair cannot be made immediately. Wheelchairs provided by the NHS will have access to repair services, but these may not be able to arrive on the same day. Wheelchairs purchased privately may have a repair package associated with them, but again same day repair is rarely possible. So, recovery of the wheelchair to the employee’s home is an essential first step. Plans should be in place to allow the employee to be accompanied home with someone able to assist with pushing the electric wheelchair into a safe location, and helping the disabled employee get into their home, and possible access an alternate wheelchair from a shed etc. An employer should have a list of taxi firms so they can send unwell employee’s home. The list should identify firms that can provide wheelchair accessible taxis. Page 19 of 30 An employer should ask all employees to provide emergency contacts. For disabled employees it may be necessary to have a longer list of contacts to allow for all circumstances and level of assistance required. Lone Working Policies must be realistic and proportionate to the risk represented. Consideration of “never works alone” should be made if a person: • Would struggle to evacuate safely alone • Is at risk of involuntary movements or falls • Is at risk of substantial loss of concentration e.g., a dissociative episode or a panic attack. Only implement “never works alone” for realistic risks. If the risk from popping in to check on progress of a process – with limited interaction with lab equipment etc. is low, then should be allowed without a partner; whilst longer periods of working in a lab can be specified as “never works alone”. Consideration should be made as to who is allocated to accompany someone according to the level of need and skills required. • Example: An employee who has occasional uncontrolled low blood sugar and so is at risk of fainting and poor cognition, may just need someone else present in the lab who would be aware that they may need to assist the disabled employee outside to get a sugary snack. • Example: An employee who struggles to control their voluntary movements may need an assistant to interact with equipment etc. under their instruction. Obviously, this assistant would need appropriate safety training, PPE, and knowledge of evacuation protocols. The assistant may be paid for from the Access to Work Scheme (ATW 2022; see Working Practice Access Guidelines Deane 2023e). • Example: Lone working protocols for home visits are adapted for a mobility impaired researcher, so that visits to homes with steps are never conducted alone. Research participants are asked specifically about steps to front door, main living area etc. • Example: An adviser with a visual impairment is sometimes required to make home visits to clients. The employer employs a support worker to assist her on these visits (EHRC 2011). The Access to Work scheme (ATW 2022) can assist with the cost of providing this type of assistance (see Working Practices Access Guidelines, Deane 2023e). However, consideration should be given to the use of assistive technology e.g., voice to text software, or of training Page 20 of 30 colleagues e.g., in key basic sign language signs essential for the running of a certain process in a lab. This could include modifying usual practice within the lab or other places of work. • Example: A worker needs to sit to conduct lab protocols in order to manage their pain and fatigue from a musculoskeletal condition. The employer provides them with an ergonomic adjustable seat that is high enough to allow them to conduct the protocol seated. They also provide them with a PPE apron to wear in addition to their lab coat so as to mitigate the risk of spills. This could include greater sensitivity to issues that may have greater impact on disabled workers. • Example: The acoustic environment of a lab may not breach noise limits but may be noisy with the running of equipment, audible indicators for end of processes, audible alarms, fans and ventilation etc. This may be particularly detrimental for autistic workers who struggle with sensory overload, or for Deaf workers who struggle to adjust their hearing aids in order to hear conversations clearly. Consideration should be given to reducing audible alarms e.g., by networking alarms to a central control panel; reducing reverberation e.g., by the use of sound baffles on walls or ceilings; moving noisy equipment into a separate soundproofed room. This could mean greater flexibility in how the tasks required are organised. • Example: Protocols have breaks scheduled within them to allow pacing of energy or concentration. • Example: Allow for flexibility in the organisation of work processes, to allow for all tasks required to be completed over a day, but the actual sequence be at the discretion of the disabled worker. This could allow them to group tasks with a specific challenge (e.g., needs high levels of concentration, needs to be completed when standing) in a way that allows them to manage their wellbeing optimally whilst still achieving all the tasks required. This could mean being more structured and explicit in the organisation of tasks or events. • Example: Provide a timed agenda for meetings and stick to this strictly. This will facilitate neurodivergent colleagues to focus and contribute better. It may be necessary to modify or adapt policies regarding PPE in order to accommodate disabilities. Consideration should be made to the maintenance, cleaning, decontamination and updating of any adapted equipment. Special consideration may be needed to facilitate the use of aids by disabled employees in restricted or hazardous environments. This could include clean rooms, use of fume hoods or Category II hoods. One solution would be to have aids that are solely used in the specialist environment. • Example: A disabled scientist is provided with a tablet computer for exclusive use within a clean room area of the lab. The tablet has voice to text software allowing the scientist to take essential notes whilst in the clean room. These are then transferred electronically to their desktop computer to allow them to work on them further etc. • Example: A wheelchair user has a separate wheelchair that they use in the clean room space. They have been tested to show that the employee can hear close conversations and all alarms when using them. They have a set of ear plugs that are used solely in the lab to reduce the risk of transferring hazardous material from one space to another. They are provided with a secure locker to store them in. Page 22 of 30 Another category of solutions is to cover the aid to prevent contamination or chemical exposure. • Example: A manual wheelchair user is provided with wheel and rim covers to reduce the risk of introduction of external contaminants into a tissue culture lab. • Example: A keyboard to a computer with assistive technology on it is provided with a plastic cover to prevent contamination and aid cleaning. Consideration should be made to the resilience of expensive personal aids such as prostheses in a lab environment Whilst it is reasonable to assume that a prosthesis is designed to cope with the hazards of conventional use (water, food spills etc), the disabled employee may need to contact the manufacturer to check its resilience to heat, pressure, or chemicals (particularly organic solvents that may dissolve or degrade plastics) specific to the lab environment and their tasks within it. For hand protheses it may be worth considering alternate tools specific to the tasks being undertaken by the disabled scientist. With robotics and 3D printing etc. it may be able to create custom designed tools that interact with the lab equipment better. It may be that a prosthesis could do certain tasks even better than a biological hand can do. Another is to adapt the aid to the environment. • Example: A clean room lab has smooth flooring to allow deep cleaning. This has a slightly higher risk of slipping than usual. So disabled scientists using walking sticks would need to have a high grip ferrule on the end of their stick. Finally aids that work in other settings may have utility in a lab environment • Example: A grab tool is useful for an employee with arthritis who struggles to pick up dropped pens etc from the floor. • Example: A visually impaired employee uses a portable text reader to read the labels on bottles of reagent or equipment. • Example: An employee who struggles to make legible notes due to poor dexterity uses a voice to text note taker and label writer. • Example: An employee with limited leg strength uses a kick step to reach a high stool to sit and work at the bench most employees stand to work at. • Example: An employer provides a support worker or arranges help from a colleague, in appropriate circumstances, for someone whose disability leads to uncertainty or lack of confidence in unfamiliar situations, such as on a training course (EHRC 2011). • Example: A man applies for a job as a lab assistant after several years of not working because of depression. He has been participating in a supported employment Page 23 of 30 scheme where he saw the post advertised. He asks the employer to let him make private phone calls during the working day to a support worker at the scheme and the employer allows him to do so as a reasonable adjustment (EHRC 2011). There has been an increase in the use of ]s by disabled people. They are used to address an increasingly diverse assistance needs. Whilst assistance dogs are traditionally viewed as being used by people with low or no vision to aid safe navigation, increasingly they are used to alert for medical conditions e.g., low blood sugar, epilepsy, or panic attacks. They may provide practical support e.g., pick items up from the floor on command, or fetch medication from a bag. Assistance dogs can sometimes be the only way to make working in a lab practical and safe for disabled people. The employer should support the training needed to ensure use of an assistance dog by a disabled person is successful. The dog, the owner, and the staff interacting with them will all need training (GDF n.d.). Structural changes required such as the provision of a safe area for the dog to rest in whilst working in the lab, a spend pound etc. are detailed in our Structural Access Guidelines (Deane 2023a). The dog’s owner will need to be able to take breaks to walk and toilet the dog. In the event of fire, protocols will need to be in place to ensure the dog is evacuated (alongside or separate to the owner) (Home Office 2007). Whilst policies should make it clear that the appropriate use of assistance dogs is supported by the employer, it is recognised that having an animal in a lab setting represents a risk that needs to be managed (ASM 2020, Redden 2021). In the first instance consideration should be given to whether the assistance dog needs to be near the disabled person at all times, or whether they can be left in a safe area (e.g., shut in an office). For example, a dog that alerts to occasional but serious medical events (e.g., epilepsy) will need to be with the disabled person at all times, but a dog that aids a visually impaired person (VIP) with navigation may not be needed in the lab as long as the layout is not changed. If the dog is left unsupervised elsewhere, they will need supplies (a mat, a water bowl etc.). Page 24 of 30 FIGURE 2: Sampson the lab dog wearing PPE: goggles, lab coat, and booties. With thanks to Empower Ability Consulting for permission to use Sampson's photo. If the dog does need to accompany their owner into the lab consideration should be given to the additional training for the dog and owner regarding lab safety e.g., trained not to pick up items from the floor except on command (ASM 2020, Redden 2021). The dog will need to wear PPE equivalent to that worn by the employees in that area and may prevent the spread of hairs and dander. The PPE may include a body suit, goggles, and booties (ISPI 2015). The PPE must have similar chemical resistance to that required for personnel PPE and be able to be decontaminated. The dog will need training on how to wear the PPE (ASM 2020, Redden 2021). Consideration should be given to where the dog will be whilst in the lab. The dog may need to be in line of sight or next to their owner. Care should be taken with regard to the trip hazard that a dog might present to other lab users. The dog should be provided with a safe area to sit whilst in the lab. This will ideally be in a low traffic area, with a washable mat. Pragmatically this may be in the bench knee nook provided for wheelchair users (ASM 2020, Redden 2021). Page 25 of 30 If the lab work includes the use of laboratory test animals (e.g., mice, rats etc) then the potential for interaction with the test animals and the assistance dog must be considered. It is possible that because test animals are usually prey species they may smell or see the assistance dog as a predator. If this would impact on the reliability of the experiments being conducted then control experiments should be conducted to check if the presence of the assistance dog has any relevant impact on the wellbeing, behaviour, or hormones (e.g., cortisol levels) of the lab animals. If proven to have such impact then consideration should be given to re-tasking animal experiments to someone else in the lab team (ASM 2020, Redden 2021). Obviously if an assistance dog behaves in such a way that poses a direct threat to the health and safety of others, if it is not housebroken, or if it not under the control of its handler, that assistance dog may be excluded from the workplace (ASM 2020, Redden 2021). It may sometimes be necessary for an employer to take a combination of steps in order to accommodate a disabled employees needs fully. • Example: A worker who is blind is given a new job with her employer in an unfamiliar part of the building. The employer: o arranges facilities for her assistance dog in the new area. o arranges for her new instructions to be in Braille; and o provides disability equality training to all staff (EHRC 2011). In some cases, a reasonable adjustment will not succeed without the co-operation of other workers. Colleagues as well as managers may therefore have an important role in helping ensure that a reasonable adjustment is carried out in practice. Subject to considerations about confidentiality, employers must ensure that this happens. It is unlikely to be a valid defence to a claim under the Equality Act to argue that an adjustment was unreasonable because staff were obstructive or unhelpful when the employer tried to implement it. An employer would at least need to be able to show that they took such behaviour seriously and dealt with it appropriately. Employers will be more likely to be able to do this if they establish and implement policies and practices that promote equity, see our Working Practice Access Guidelines (Deane 2023e). • Example: An employer ensures that an autistic worker has a structured working day as a reasonable adjustment. As part of this adjustment, it is the responsibility of the employer to ensure that other workers co-operate with this arrangement (EHRC 2011). Page 26 of 30 4 How these guidelines were created To remove the barriers to accessing life, so people can express their brilliance. We genuinely believe that anyone can work in science. We believe that having a diverse workforce enhances the quality and utility of the science created. The core workplace of science is the laboratory. In these guidelines “Labs" refers to laboratories, manufacturing and production lines, engineering facilities, etc. “Scientists” refers to scientists, technologists, engineers, mathematicians, and healthcare professionals etc. “Disabled” relates to people who are disabled, D/deaf, or have long term health conditions (both physical and mental), illnesses, or injuries, that have a significant impact on their ability to carry out everyday tasks. The aim was to create a set of documents that would provide a pragmatic and useful guide on to how to create an accessible lab workplace. We wished to accumulate relevant guidelines for lab contexts, edit them for relevancy, expand them in order to be as comprehensive as possible, and share them with the scientific community. The guidelines are mostly created from previously published work, which we cite. We wanted to provide guidelines for the whole of the lab work ecosystem, and to consider all types of impairments and disabilities. 1 Structural access – physical design of laboratory and fixed equipment (e.g., hoods, sinks etc.) 2 Equipment access – design and use of movable equipment (e.g., microscopes, centrifuges, PCR machines etc.) 3 Protocol access – adaptation of lab protocols to accommodate access needs (e.g., seated working, evacuation protocols, lone working etc.) 4 Dissemination access – work done in laboratories must be shared with the wider world. Access issues can be encountered in consultation and dissemination events, meetings, conferences, the publication of work on web pages and in journal articles. Page 27 of 30 5 General working practices access – adaptation of usual HR and working practices (e.g., part time or flexible hours), assisting disabled staff to access to relevant benefits, accessible transport and parking etc. A significant proportion of the Access All Areas in Labs team have disabilities themselves, with lived experience of impairments in mobility, vision, stamina, dexterity, mental wellbeing, cognitive focus, and a range of neurodiversities. They have worked in microbiological, immunological, engineering, electronic, clinical trial, and pharmacy settings as students, researchers, principal investigators, technicians, and administrators. We searched scientific databases (MEDLINE, EMBASE); grey literature; professional magazines; online resources; relevant charities and trade unions; centres for disability studies; consultants that support disabled researchers and employers. We snowballed contacts and resources from the originally identified literature. We also conducted a survey of people with an interest in lab access about barriers and solutions to lab access (Deane 2023d) along with a set of case study interviews examining solutions to lab access (AAAiLabs 2023). We identified a key guideline or two at the start of the creation of each of our guidelines. This would then be combined with information from other guidelines, data from the survey and case studies, and combined with the team’s lived expertise to allow us to provide comprehensive guidelines with exemplars of implementation solutions across a range of settings and impairments.
