### 1.1 Principles of disability accommodation
It is important to note that it is not unlawful for an employer to treat a disabled person more favourably compared to a non-disabled person (EHRC 2011). • All employers have a legal duty under the Equality Act 2010 to proactively make reasonable adjustments to remove, reduce or prevent any disadvantages that disabled workers face (TUC 2019). Failing to provide reasonable adjustments may be unlawful. • All workers deserve the opportunity to realise their full potential (TUC 2019). • In order to achieve equality for disabled people work may need to be organised differently, support provided, and barriers removed (TUC 2019). • All reasonable steps must be taken to ensure that policies, practices, and culture do not discriminate against disabled people (TUC 2019). • Each person is unique and that there can be a high degree of overlap between multiple conditions. Consequently, any support needs must be identified and implemented on the basis of personal evaluation and individual need (TUC 2019). The employer should commit to: • Proactively work to eliminate barriers (including prejudice) that disabled people face in the workplace (TUC 2019). • Raise awareness of the full range of disabilities including those that are often overlooked, for example: mental health conditions, dyslexia or other neurodivergent conditions (TUC 2019). • Consider changes made in response to requests for reasonable adjustments (TUC 2019). • Take immediate steps to eliminate potentially discriminatory practices in employment that can arise throughout the course of normal day-to-day workplace activities (TUC 2019).

### 1.2 The social model of disability
These guidelines are informed by the Social Model of Disability (Oliver 1990, Scope n.d.). This proposes that the majority of disability is caused by a lack of accommodation for impairments and differences. For example, a wheelchair user cannot get into a building because there are steps before the entrance. This is disabling not because the person is using a wheelchair but due to a lack of provision of a ramp. The responsibility for access lies with the owners of the building, not with the disabled person. “Barriers can make it impossible or very difficult to access jobs, buildings or services, but the biggest barrier of all is the problem of people’s attitude to Page 7 of 30 disability. Removing the barriers is the best way to include millions of disabled people in our society” (TUC 2019).

### 1.3 The duty to make reasonable adjustments
All employers have a legal duty under the Equality Act 2010 to proactively make reasonable adjustments to remove, reduce or prevent any disadvantages that disabled workers face (TUC 2019). In order to achieve equity for disabled people, work may need to be organised differently, support provided, and barriers removed.

### 1.4 The benefits of accessible labs
Labs are often designed without consideration to disability access due to the historic assumption that disabled scientists could not work safely in such environments. If disabled people’s needs are not designed into work and workplaces, then few disabled people will be able to work there. This is part of why there is a significant under representation of disabled people working in science, technology, engineering, and maths (STEM). Whilst approximately 22% of the UK adult population of working age are disabled, only around 3.8% of UK STEM academics are identified as disabled (Joice 2021). The lack of diversity in research participants and scientists is a factor in wasteful research due to serious flaws in prioritisation, design, sampling, analysis and interpretation, etc. (Glasziou 2018; Macleod 2014; JLA 2023). Research that is informed by a diverse multidisciplinary team is better able to ensure practicality, utility, and impact (Deane 2014 and 2019, Schroeder 2022). The opportunity cost of not having disabled scientists with their diversity of experience and expertise is likely to be significant. Additionally, most disabilities are acquired; the loss of highly qualified scientists from the field when they acquire a disability is a substantial loss on the investment in their training. We start with the assumption that all disabled scientists are able to work in labs, if the labs are designed with their access needs met. Safety issues can be designed “out” of the labs; either in the structural or equipment design or in the protocols used. Accessibility also includes the design of the work processes, staff knowledge and attitudes. Accessible labs will allow a greater proportion of disabled scientists to be trained and work in lab settings in a safe and comfortable manner. We genuinely believe this improved diversity in the workforce will enhance the quality and potential profitability of the work done in laboratory settings. Page 8 of 30

### 2.1 Duty to make reasonable adjustments.
The duty to make reasonable adjustments is a cornerstone of the Equality Act 2010 and requires employers to take positive steps to ensure that disabled people can access and progress in employment. This goes beyond simply avoiding treating disabled workers, job applicants and potential job applicants unfavourably and means taking additional steps to which non-disabled workers and applicants are not entitled (EHRC 2011). It is important to understand that treating a disabled employee more favourably in order to accommodate their impairment and ensure they are able to do their job safely and effectively is allowed. Treating all employees exactly the same, irrespective of disability, may well be discriminatory and in breach of the Equality Act 2010.

### 2.2 Relevance of reasonable adjustments
Employers can often prevent unfavourable treatment which would amount to discrimination arising from disability by taking prompt action to identify and implement reasonable adjustments (EHRC 2011) If an employer has failed to make a reasonable adjustment which would have prevented or minimised the unfavourable treatment, it will be very difficult for them to show that the treatment was objectively justified (EHRC 2011).

### 2.3 Benefits of implementing the provisions of the Equality Act
Employers who use positive action measures or implement reasonable adjustments may find this brings benefits to their own organisation or business (EHRC 2011). Benefits could include: • a wider pool of talented, skilled and experienced people from which to recruit (EHRC 2011) • retention of highly trained staff, and so a reduction in the time and money represented by having to recruit new staff for a position currently filled by a disabled member of staff • a dynamic and challenging workforce able to respond to changes (EHRC 2011) • a better understanding of foreign/global markets (EHRC 2011) • a better understanding of the needs of a more diverse range of customers – both nationally and internationally (EHRC 2011) • greater insight into the challenges faced by disabled people so products and services can be designed to ensure they do not include barriers to their use. • Structural access changes often have “wash-over” benefits for all staff e.g., powered doors mean trolleys can be manoeuvred more easily. Page 9 of 30 • Training and policy changes can mean everyone’s diversities are better understood and accommodated e.g., flexible use of working from home is used by staff with disabilities, those with caring responsibilities, and by everyone who has the occasional need to be at home e.g., to wait for a repairman to arrive. • A clear demonstration of an employer’s respect for their staff’s needs in practical terms.

### 2.4 Consultation
Consultation must always be undertaken when planning new buildings, planning on the purchase of new equipment, or revising policies and practices. If there is a specific disabled member of staff who will be impacted by the changes, they must be consulted for ideas about and approval of access solutions particularly relevant to their impairments. However, the employer should always be aware of their need to pre-emptively consider access for all types of impairments. Therefore, it is recommended that they take the advice of trade unions, disabled staff groups, and potentially charities or access consultants to ensure they maximise accessibility. Additionally, it is strongly recommended that the employer consults with: • the staff who will be using the space, equipment, or new policy • the cleaning and maintenance teams to ensure it works well for everyone.

### 2.5 Policy regarding the funding and prioritisation of access solutions
New builds and new equipment should be specified to the highest possible access standard (please see Structural Access Guidelines and Equipment Access Guidelines Deane 2023a and 2023b). Access should have a similar priority in budgeting and design as other legislative requirements e.g., health and safety or building standards. It is essential that employers regard access for all types of disability irrespective of the access needs of the people currently using that space • Example: A hospital is replacing the front door of a building which accesses laboratory services. The hospital does not put in motors to allow the doors to open automatically because “no one needs that, we don’t have any patients in this building, and we could power up the door if we were asked.” This could be found to be a breach of the Equality Act which requires pre-emptive action to provide access where reasonable. Adding motors to the doors when they were being replaced is the cheapest time to do so, retrofitting access solution is always more expensive. Additionally, it would take time to fit door motors, which could prevent a new disabled employee from easily entering the building for work whilst waiting for them to be fitted. Page 10 of 30 It is recognised that existing buildings may present substantially greater challenges when trying to improve access. However, there should be policies that require access improvements to be considered whenever any renovation or even redecoration of an existing building occurs. • Example: The electrical team replace white facias of sockets or light switches with coloured ones that contrast with the wall colour in order to enhance visual access (Structural Access Guidelines, Deane 2023a). They do this anytime they need to replace a fascia. • Example: The decorating team paint the walls behind the toilet and sink in a contrasting colour in all the toilet facilities (both accessible and standard) in order to enhance visual access (Structural Access Guidelines, Deane 2023a). Page 11 of 30

### 3.1 Use of premises adjusted to maximise access
Many of the accessibility improvements suggested in our Structural Access Guidelines (Deane 2023a) and Equipment Access Guidelines (Deane 2023b) will only work if maintained, cleaned, and used appropriately. Policies and protocols should ensure access adaptations to premises: • Have clear guidance on their appropriate use e.g., safe working load signs on stair lifts • Have clear instructions on who to contact in the event of breakdown, damage, or cleaning need • Are checked on a regular schedule to ensure they work appropriately e.g., hearing loops, alarms in accessible toilets • Are included in the area’s regular cleaning schedule • Are given high priority for repair and remedial cleaning • Have a regular schedule of maintenance

#### 3.1.1 Alarms
Red alarm cords are provided in spaces such as toilets and showers because these areas represent high risk areas for falls for people with mobility impairments etc. There must be a clear protocol for how alarms are maintained and responded to. Red cord cards are highly effective at reducing the tendency for red cords to be “tidied away” and thus removing their utility. They can be obtained from Euan’s Guide (2015 https://www.euansguide.com/news/red-cord-card/). FIGURE 1 A picture of Euan’s Guide’s Red Cord Card Additionally, there must be a protocol so that an alarm notifies appropriate people and is responded to immediately. For example, the alarm sounds at reception during office hours, Page 12 of 30 but is diverted to security out of hours. Both the reception and security teams are aware of how to override the door lock, and to sensitively respond to someone in distress. Tests should be run at least twice annually to check that the alarm works and that it is responded to promptly.

#### 3.1.2 Out of order communication strategy
There should be a clear communication strategy to ensure that users are informed when access features are out of use e.g., lifts, accessible toilets. For example, emails and/or text alerts to all workers with a personal emergency evacuation plan due to their mobility impairments informing them when a lift is out of order. When considering the information to be relayed consideration should be given to providing: • Information on the piece of equipment that is out of order • Its location • The time/date it went out of order • The expected time/date that it is hoped to be repaired by • Contact details for any queries • Alternate equipment or routes that can be used in the meantime – with location and possibly maps The communication plan should include options to send another message to appropriate disabled staff once the facility is back in working order, or if the repair is delayed. Consideration must be given to ensuring the format is accessible for everyone receiving the messages. The Access All Areas in Labs Dissemination Access Guideline (2023) provides detailed information on how to do this. • Example: Voice messages may be left for someone with dyslexia in preference to (or in addition to) e-mail messages. Policies should escalate the priority of the repair if it is not achieved within a previously agreed timeframe e.g., within two working days for the repair of an accessible toilet. Records should be kept allowing tracking of time out of action for access facilities so as to identify if this is likely to have had negative impact on disabled staff’s ability to work well or access certain facilities. A reasonable accommodation would be to record any impact of these facility breakdowns so that they can be taken into account when conducting an appraisal of a disabled employee’s work, or when organising alternate work practices e.g., working from home. • Example: A disabled employee uses a wheelchair for mobility. Their lab is on the second floor. There are two lifts, one at each end of a long building, and the accessible toilet is on the ground floor. The lift that is closest to the disabled employee’s lab and the accessible toilet downstairs is frequently broken for days or weeks on end. This means that the employee is regularly having to take long breaks in order to use the far lift to reach the accessible toilet. He raises this in his Page 13 of 30 performance review, and it is agreed that the impact of this extra travel time will be taken into account when assessing his efficiency. A query is also raised with Estates regarding what plans are in place to permanently resolve the lift’s reliability. • Example: It is agreed that an employee with poor mobility who works on the third floor, can work from home on days where planned maintenance of the lift is scheduled. If the lift goes out of order, Estates send out a message to their “high priority lift list” to let them know how long the repair is likely to take. If it is predicted to take more than half a day, it has been agreed that the employee can leave early and work from home until the lift is repaired.

#### 3.1.3 Cleaning and tidying
Particular care should be paid to the cleanliness of accessible facilities. Staff that use them often have no other option but to continue to use them even if they find them in an unclean state. • Example: After complaints from a wheelchair user about the lift smelling of rotting garbage, the cleaning team add a sanitising step to clean the lift after it has been used to remove garbage bags from upper floors. Unfortunately, the extra space that is provided in accessible facilities can be viewed as storage space by staff unaware that the space is essential to allow wheelchairs to turn, or to have space for the assistance of carers. It is not uncommon for disabled staff to find spare chairs, coat racks, mops, buckets etc. stored in accessible toilets. Cleaning staff are particularly important in checking on the appropriate use of the facilities, as they should be checking on the cleanliness of these at regular intervals (just as they do for the standard toilet facilities). The cleaning teams should be empowered to remove anything inappropriately stored in toilets and let the building manager know of the issue.

#### 3.1.4 Ensuring ongoing access during building works
It can be challenging to ensure access is retained whilst building works are ongoing. Consideration should be given to whether key routes (e.g., step free) will be blocked, or key facilities (e.g., lifts) will be put out of action during the works. Staff should be consulted to identify alternate routes or facilities well in advance of the works starting. Clear signage should give notice of the works planned and identify the person to be contacted in the event of queries. Disabled staff who cannot access a certain area of a building or facility that is essential for the conduct of their role, should have their work re-evaluated and adjusted to accommodate this temporary lack of access e.g., changed to work from home, certain tasks handed over to others in the team etc. All workers conducting the building works (including contractors) should be aware of the primacy of ensuring ongoing access. • Example: All contractors are required to sign an agreement emphasising that inappropriate use of accessible parking bays is always unacceptable. Security is Page 14 of 30 aware that anyone inappropriately using an accessible parking bay should be given a parking fine, and that if it is a contractor’s vehicle, they should contact Estates who will follow up with a formal complaint to the company in addition to the fine. • Example: Skips for building rubble are required. The works will block one building entrance and the skips will be placed over three accessible parking bays associated with this entrance. Three additional accessible parking bays will be marked out next to the alternate entrance to the building for the duration of the works.

#### 3.1.5 Accommodations in policies regarding use of facilities Policies can be adapted such that they prioritise disabled staff so as to facilitate access.
• Example: Senior staff are usually the only staff provided with parking spaces on site. A disabled worker with mobility impairments may be provided with a designated parking space close to the building irrespective of their seniority. If they use a wheelchair or other mobility equipment, then a larger accessible parking bay should be provided.

### 3.2 Information provision
The Structural Access Guideline (Deane 2023a) provides detailed descriptions of signage for navigation and identification of accessible facilities and equipment (e.g., lifts, hearing loops). The Dissemination Access Guideline (Deane 2023c) provides detailed descriptions of what information is need and how to provide information on documents and web pages in accessible formats. In particular we recommend providing access information on a dedicated webpage that is easy to find from the front page of the company’s or venue’s website. There really is no such thing as “too much” access information. • Example: Accessible toilet information on a company’s web page includes: o A map of the location o Photos to aid identification of location and content of toilet facilities o Dimensions of the toilet, including which side the transfer is on o Contact details for any concerns regarding cleaning or maintenance. If rooms, facilities or equipment can be booked by staff then access information should be provided in the booking form e.g., step free venue, availability of hearing loop, ability to book out “easy grip” versions of equipment. It is recommended that booking systems encourage best practice behaviours e.g., allowing the room booking system to select only “fully accessible” rooms e.g., with step free access, with hearing loops and microphones; and that the use of these rooms is a mandatory requirement for public events.

### 3.3 Allocating some of the disabled person’s duties to another worker
An employer might reallocate minor or subsidiary duties to another worker as a disabled worker has difficulty doing them because of his disability (EHRC 2011). Page 15 of 30 • Example: For example, the job involves occasionally going up a set of stairs to access the top of a vat to take samples. The employer transfers this work away from a worker whose disability involves mobility impairment. • Example: A lab technician is tasked to setting up a workstation with relevant solutions so that a disabled worker can just program the assistive robot to run a set of protocols and supervise its conduct.

### 3.4 Altering the disabled worker’s hours of work
An employer should consider if allowing a disabled person to work flexible hours might mitigate some of their impairment. For example, enabling a worker to have additional breaks to overcome fatigue arising from their disability. It could also include permitting parttime working or different working hours to avoid the need to travel in the rush hour if this creates a problem related to an impairment. A phased return to work with a gradual buildup of hours might also be appropriate in some circumstances (EHRC 2011). • Example: A biomedical lab runs a shift system with staff rotating through “early”, “late”, and “night” shifts for two weeks at a time. A disabled scientist with epilepsy and autism struggles to maintain their medication and sleep routines to a sufficiently stringent standard to prevent fitting. They are allowed to work an “early” shift permanently.

### 3.5 Assigning the disabled worker to a different place of work or arranging home or hybrid working
This accommodation can be hugely important to allow a disabled worker to optimise the management of their symptoms, particularly fatigue. Travelling in and out of work and moving around a workplace can create excessive fatigue in people with energy limiting conditions (Hale 2021). • Example: An employer relocates the workstation of a newly disabled worker (who now uses a wheelchair) from an inaccessible third floor office to an accessible one on the ground floor. It may be reasonable to move his place of work to other premises of the same employer if the first building is inaccessible (EHRC 2011). • Example: Allowing the worker to work from home for some or all of their role might also be a reasonable adjustment for the employer to make (EHRC 2011). Consideration should be made to ensure online, or hybrid meetings have appropriate access arranged (e.g., sign language interpreters). Hybrid meetings need to be appropriately facilitated to ensure equality of contribution of those online and in person (Dissemination Access Guidelines, Deane 2023c). Page 16 of 30

### 3.6 Allowing the disabled worker to be absent during working hours for rehabilitation, assessment, or treatment
Absence for rehabilitation, assessment or treatment should not be regarded as the same as standard sick leave. Policies should be in place to identify that this leave is disability-related and comes under specific policies that ensure equity. • Example: An employer allows a person who has become disabled more time off work than would be allowed to non-disabled workers to enable him to have rehabilitation training. A similar adjustment may be appropriate if a disability worsens or if a disabled person needs occasional treatment anyway (EHRC 2011).

### 3.7 Giving, or arranging for, training or mentoring (whether for the disabled person or any other worker)
This could be training in particular pieces of equipment which the disabled person uses, or an alteration to the standard workplace training to reflect the worker’s particular disability (EHRC 2011). Research has identified that employees with protected characteristics are at highest risk of suffering discriminatory or bullying behaviour (Wellcome 2020; Deane 2023d). Therefore, it is strongly recommended that employers provide training aimed at raising awareness and changing the workplace culture e.g., training in preventing disability discrimination and promoting allyship. • Example: All workers are trained in the use of a particular machine, but an employer provides slightly different or longer training for a worker with restricted hand or arm movements (EHRC 2011). • Example: An employer might also provide training in additional software for a visually impaired worker so that he can use a computer with speech output (EHRC 2011). • Example: A disabled employee needs to use an Evacuation Chair in the event of fire. The disabled employee should be given an opportunity to try using the Evacuation Chair with no time pressure. Fire wardens and anyone else who it is reasonable to assume might be required to aid in an evacuation (e.g., security team) should be trained on how to use the chair.

### 3.8 Modifying fire evacuation procedures
Any worker with an impairment that might interfere with their safe evacuation from a building should be provided with a personal emergency evacuation plan (PEEP) (Home Office 2007). This usually includes people with mobility, hearing or visual impairments. However, consideration should be given to other impairments e.g., neurodiversity, where navigation under stress and sensory overload may be problematic. Consideration should be given to additional training needed – both for the disabled member of staff and fire wardens etc. Page 17 of 30 Evacuation protocols may require the disabled worker to carry a mobile phone with them so they can inform security of their location in the event of fire. Some disabled people may only be able to be in a building, or certain areas of a building, when accompanied by another person (who is responsible for assisting their evacuation). It should also be remembered that what a disabled person is prepared to do in exceptional circumstances may differ significantly from what they can reasonably manage in their everyday activities (Home Office 2007). Fire evacuation drills need to balance the relative risks of knowing how to evacuate the building speedily with the risk of the evacuation process itself – especially for workers with mobility impairments. For example, the risk of transferring to an Evacuation Chair from a wheelchair is often not trivial and may risk falls and injuries. Workers who need to use an Evacuation Chair or Powered Stair Climber to aid evacuation from upper floors may be allowed to remain in the stair well for fire drills having contacted security or fire wardens. They would not actually evacuate from the building for the drill. However, the disabled worker should be trained in how to use the Evacuation Chair or Powered Stair Climber (e.g. Super Trac 2021) at another instance. This training should be without time pressure, and with sufficient staff to assist. In the case of an Evacuation Chair the training will aim to ensure the disabled member of staff to learn how to transfer safely from a wheelchair into an Evacuation Chair, and for their assistants (if any) to learn how to safely assist with this. Should a disabled member of staff require assistance to transfer safely then it is likely they will need a safe working protocol that requires them to be accompanied by a suitably trained assistant at all times. In the case of a Powered Stair Climber the disabled person will need to learn how to manoeuvre their wheelchair onto the platform safely. As a Powered Stair Climber does not require a disabled person to transfer out of their wheelchair in order to be evacuated, this option is safer and accommodates a wider range of impairments than an Evacuation Chair. However it is recognised that it does require a staircase with good clearance (1600mm x 1600mm) and is considerably more expensive. Disabled staff who cannot hear fire alarms must have a PEEP created for them. Consideration should be given to the installation of dual alert fire alarm systems (audio and visual alarms). Consideration should be given to the use of a mobile phone app that vibrates in response to alarms. However, this sort of app may be confused by the “process finished” audible alerts from the lab equipment and effectively give false alarms, so this should be tested for utility in the workplace. • Example: A senior manager who is deaf is required to work late and be in the office early on occasion. The office has a 24-hour security presence, and it is necessary for all staff to sign in and out at the security point. An arrangement is made that, should an alarm be raised out of hours when the manager is present, the security guard will contact the manager on their textphone to alert them of the emergency. This was Page 18 of 30 built into the instruction manual on means of escape procedures for all security staff (Home Office 2007).

#### 3.8.1 Creation of non-emergency evacuation procedures
There are a number of potential circumstances in which disabled people may need additional assistance to get themselves and/or their equipment out of the building. For example, an employee becomes unwell and unstable on their feet whilst on the upper floor of a building without a lift or the lift breaks down and a person with limited mobility needs to leave the building from a higher floor. In these cases, it is appropriate to use Evacuation Chairs to help remove the employee safely from the upper floors to the ground floor of the building. Any walking aids should be brought down with them, so they can walk as safely as possible once they reach ground level. Manual wheelchairs are usually light enough to be a single person lift (i.e., less than 25kg). However, they can be an awkward shape so consideration should have been given to the safe removal of a manual wheelchair from a building if the lift is out of action. Another circumstance is that the lift breaks down and an electric wheelchair user needs to leave the building from a higher floor. So obviously you can start by evacuating the disabled person in an Evacuation Chair to the ground floor. It is getting their wheelchair to the ground floor as well that is the challenge. A couple of key facts are important to this example. 1. In a non-emergency evacuation it is essential that a wheelchair user is not left without their wheelchair for an extended period of time. 2. Electric wheelchairs can be large and heavy (commonly between 120-150kg); and the weight is unevenly distributed. It is likely that a plan will have to be created for each wheelchair as they vary substantially in size and weight. Wheelchairs have tie down loops for use in vehicles, so these are likely to be a safe place to affix straps to aid removal of the wheelchair down the stairs. A final circumstance that may need consideration is if an electric wheelchair breaks down on an upper floor. As discussed before an electric wheelchair is essential for the wellbeing of a disabled person and is heavy. Whilst such a chair can be pushed manually to a lift and potentially up a ramp into a taxi or the employee’s wheelchair accessible vehicle; it will be heavy and unwieldy. It should be assumed that a repair cannot be made immediately. Wheelchairs provided by the NHS will have access to repair services, but these may not be able to arrive on the same day. Wheelchairs purchased privately may have a repair package associated with them, but again same day repair is rarely possible. So, recovery of the wheelchair to the employee’s home is an essential first step. Plans should be in place to allow the employee to be accompanied home with someone able to assist with pushing the electric wheelchair into a safe location, and helping the disabled employee get into their home, and possible access an alternate wheelchair from a shed etc. An employer should have a list of taxi firms so they can send unwell employee’s home. The list should identify firms that can provide wheelchair accessible taxis. Page 19 of 30 An employer should ask all employees to provide emergency contacts. For disabled employees it may be necessary to have a longer list of contacts to allow for all circumstances and level of assistance required.

### 3.9 Modifying lone working policies
Lone Working Policies must be realistic and proportionate to the risk represented. Consideration of “never works alone” should be made if a person: • Would struggle to evacuate safely alone • Is at risk of involuntary movements or falls • Is at risk of substantial loss of concentration e.g., a dissociative episode or a panic attack. Only implement “never works alone” for realistic risks. If the risk from popping in to check on progress of a process – with limited interaction with lab equipment etc. is low, then should be allowed without a partner; whilst longer periods of working in a lab can be specified as “never works alone”. Consideration should be made as to who is allocated to accompany someone according to the level of need and skills required. • Example: An employee who has occasional uncontrolled low blood sugar and so is at risk of fainting and poor cognition, may just need someone else present in the lab who would be aware that they may need to assist the disabled employee outside to get a sugary snack. • Example: An employee who struggles to control their voluntary movements may need an assistant to interact with equipment etc. under their instruction. Obviously, this assistant would need appropriate safety training, PPE, and knowledge of evacuation protocols. The assistant may be paid for from the Access to Work Scheme (ATW 2022; see Working Practice Access Guidelines Deane 2023e). • Example: Lone working protocols for home visits are adapted for a mobility impaired researcher, so that visits to homes with steps are never conducted alone. Research participants are asked specifically about steps to front door, main living area etc.

### 3.10 Employing a support worker to assist a disabled worker
• Example: An adviser with a visual impairment is sometimes required to make home visits to clients. The employer employs a support worker to assist her on these visits (EHRC 2011).

### 3.11 Providing a reader, interpreter, or note taker
The Access to Work scheme (ATW 2022) can assist with the cost of providing this type of assistance (see Working Practices Access Guidelines, Deane 2023e). However, consideration should be given to the use of assistive technology e.g., voice to text software, or of training Page 20 of 30 colleagues e.g., in key basic sign language signs essential for the running of a certain process in a lab.

### 3.12 Modifying work procedures
This could include modifying usual practice within the lab or other places of work. • Example: A worker needs to sit to conduct lab protocols in order to manage their pain and fatigue from a musculoskeletal condition. The employer provides them with an ergonomic adjustable seat that is high enough to allow them to conduct the protocol seated. They also provide them with a PPE apron to wear in addition to their lab coat so as to mitigate the risk of spills. This could include greater sensitivity to issues that may have greater impact on disabled workers. • Example: The acoustic environment of a lab may not breach noise limits but may be noisy with the running of equipment, audible indicators for end of processes, audible alarms, fans and ventilation etc. This may be particularly detrimental for autistic workers who struggle with sensory overload, or for Deaf workers who struggle to adjust their hearing aids in order to hear conversations clearly. Consideration should be given to reducing audible alarms e.g., by networking alarms to a central control panel; reducing reverberation e.g., by the use of sound baffles on walls or ceilings; moving noisy equipment into a separate soundproofed room. This could mean greater flexibility in how the tasks required are organised. • Example: Protocols have breaks scheduled within them to allow pacing of energy or concentration. • Example: Allow for flexibility in the organisation of work processes, to allow for all tasks required to be completed over a day, but the actual sequence be at the discretion of the disabled worker. This could allow them to group tasks with a specific challenge (e.g., needs high levels of concentration, needs to be completed when standing) in a way that allows them to manage their wellbeing optimally whilst still achieving all the tasks required. This could mean being more structured and explicit in the organisation of tasks or events. • Example: Provide a timed agenda for meetings and stick to this strictly. This will facilitate neurodivergent colleagues to focus and contribute better.

### 3.13 Modifying personal protective equipment (PPE)
It may be necessary to modify or adapt policies regarding PPE in order to accommodate disabilities. Page 21 of 30 • Example: A disabled worker with severe asthma does not need to wear FFP2 grade masks when working in an enclosed area. • Example: Other lab workers may be asked to wear FFP2 masks when working in an enclosed lab with a disabled worker who is severely immunocompromised due to the ongoing chemotherapy treatment of their cancer. This will enhance their protection from airborne infectious agents e.g., coronavirus. • Example: A wheelchair user wears a protective apron in addition to the usual lab coat. • Example: An assistance dog is provided with PPE equivalent to that provided for the employees in a given area. (See below for specific advice on assistance dogs). • Example: A employee who uses a below the elbow arm prosthesis is provided with extra long gloves to protect the whole prosthesis from contamination.

### 3.13 Acquiring or modifying equipment
Detailed guidance on the design, adaptation, and use of equipment by disabled workers is provided in the Equipment Access Guideline (Deane 2023b). Consideration should be made to the maintenance, cleaning, decontamination and updating of any adapted equipment.

### 3.14 Use of aids in restricted or hazardous environments
Special consideration may be needed to facilitate the use of aids by disabled employees in restricted or hazardous environments. This could include clean rooms, use of fume hoods or Category II hoods. One solution would be to have aids that are solely used in the specialist environment. • Example: A disabled scientist is provided with a tablet computer for exclusive use within a clean room area of the lab. The tablet has voice to text software allowing the scientist to take essential notes whilst in the clean room. These are then transferred electronically to their desktop computer to allow them to work on them further etc. • Example: A wheelchair user has a separate wheelchair that they use in the clean room space. The employee transfers from their everyday wheelchair to the clean room chair in the changing room area, which has a hoist to ensure this can be done safely. Consideration was made when purchasing the clean room wheelchair as to its potential decontamination. A waterproof and chemical resistant cover was created for the seat cushion. • Example: An autistic employee uses noise reducing ear plugs. They have been tested to show that the employee can hear close conversations and all alarms when using them. They have a set of ear plugs that are used solely in the lab to reduce the risk of transferring hazardous material from one space to another. They are provided with a secure locker to store them in. Page 22 of 30 Another category of solutions is to cover the aid to prevent contamination or chemical exposure. • Example: A manual wheelchair user is provided with wheel and rim covers to reduce the risk of introduction of external contaminants into a tissue culture lab. • Example: A keyboard to a computer with assistive technology on it is provided with a plastic cover to prevent contamination and aid cleaning. Consideration should be made to the resilience of expensive personal aids such as prostheses in a lab environment Whilst it is reasonable to assume that a prosthesis is designed to cope with the hazards of conventional use (water, food spills etc), the disabled employee may need to contact the manufacturer to check its resilience to heat, pressure, or chemicals (particularly organic solvents that may dissolve or degrade plastics) specific to the lab environment and their tasks within it. For hand protheses it may be worth considering alternate tools specific to the tasks being undertaken by the disabled scientist. With robotics and 3D printing etc. it may be able to create custom designed tools that interact with the lab equipment better. It may be that a prosthesis could do certain tasks even better than a biological hand can do. Another is to adapt the aid to the environment. • Example: A clean room lab has smooth flooring to allow deep cleaning. This has a slightly higher risk of slipping than usual. So disabled scientists using walking sticks would need to have a high grip ferrule on the end of their stick. Finally aids that work in other settings may have utility in a lab environment • Example: A grab tool is useful for an employee with arthritis who struggles to pick up dropped pens etc from the floor. • Example: A visually impaired employee uses a portable text reader to read the labels on bottles of reagent or equipment. • Example: An employee who struggles to make legible notes due to poor dexterity uses a voice to text note taker and label writer. • Example: An employee with limited leg strength uses a kick step to reach a high stool to sit and work at the bench most employees stand to work at.

### 3.15 Providing supervision or other support
• Example: An employer provides a support worker or arranges help from a colleague, in appropriate circumstances, for someone whose disability leads to uncertainty or lack of confidence in unfamiliar situations, such as on a training course (EHRC 2011).

### 3.16 Participating in supported employment schemes, such as Workstep
• Example: A man applies for a job as a lab assistant after several years of not working because of depression. He has been participating in a supported employment Page 23 of 30 scheme where he saw the post advertised. He asks the employer to let him make private phone calls during the working day to a support worker at the scheme and the employer allows him to do so as a reasonable adjustment (EHRC 2011).

### 3.17 Ensuring that assistance dog policies are supportive
There has been an increase in the use of ]s by disabled people. They are used to address an increasingly diverse assistance needs. Whilst assistance dogs are traditionally viewed as being used by people with low or no vision to aid safe navigation, increasingly they are used to alert for medical conditions e.g., low blood sugar, epilepsy, or panic attacks. They may provide practical support e.g., pick items up from the floor on command, or fetch medication from a bag. Assistance dogs can sometimes be the only way to make working in a lab practical and safe for disabled people. The employer should support the training needed to ensure use of an assistance dog by a disabled person is successful. The dog, the owner, and the staff interacting with them will all need training (GDF n.d.). Structural changes required such as the provision of a safe area for the dog to rest in whilst working in the lab, a spend pound etc. are detailed in our Structural Access Guidelines (Deane 2023a). The dog’s owner will need to be able to take breaks to walk and toilet the dog. In the event of fire, protocols will need to be in place to ensure the dog is evacuated (alongside or separate to the owner) (Home Office 2007). Whilst policies should make it clear that the appropriate use of assistance dogs is supported by the employer, it is recognised that having an animal in a lab setting represents a risk that needs to be managed (ASM 2020, Redden 2021). In the first instance consideration should be given to whether the assistance dog needs to be near the disabled person at all times, or whether they can be left in a safe area (e.g., shut in an office). For example, a dog that alerts to occasional but serious medical events (e.g., epilepsy) will need to be with the disabled person at all times, but a dog that aids a visually impaired person (VIP) with navigation may not be needed in the lab as long as the layout is not changed. If the dog is left unsupervised elsewhere, they will need supplies (a mat, a water bowl etc.). Page 24 of 30 FIGURE 2: Sampson the lab dog wearing PPE: goggles, lab coat, and booties. With thanks to Empower Ability Consulting for permission to use Sampson's photo. If the dog does need to accompany their owner into the lab consideration should be given to the additional training for the dog and owner regarding lab safety e.g., trained not to pick up items from the floor except on command (ASM 2020, Redden 2021). The dog will need to wear PPE equivalent to that worn by the employees in that area and may prevent the spread of hairs and dander. The PPE may include a body suit, goggles, and booties (ISPI 2015). The PPE must have similar chemical resistance to that required for personnel PPE and be able to be decontaminated. The dog will need training on how to wear the PPE (ASM 2020, Redden 2021). Consideration should be given to where the dog will be whilst in the lab. The dog may need to be in line of sight or next to their owner. Care should be taken with regard to the trip hazard that a dog might present to other lab users. The dog should be provided with a safe area to sit whilst in the lab. This will ideally be in a low traffic area, with a washable mat. Pragmatically this may be in the bench knee nook provided for wheelchair users (ASM 2020, Redden 2021). Page 25 of 30 If the lab work includes the use of laboratory test animals (e.g., mice, rats etc) then the potential for interaction with the test animals and the assistance dog must be considered. It is possible that because test animals are usually prey species they may smell or see the assistance dog as a predator. If this would impact on the reliability of the experiments being conducted then control experiments should be conducted to check if the presence of the assistance dog has any relevant impact on the wellbeing, behaviour, or hormones (e.g., cortisol levels) of the lab animals. If proven to have such impact then consideration should be given to re-tasking animal experiments to someone else in the lab team (ASM 2020, Redden 2021). Obviously if an assistance dog behaves in such a way that poses a direct threat to the health and safety of others, if it is not housebroken, or if it not under the control of its handler, that assistance dog may be excluded from the workplace (ASM 2020, Redden 2021).

### 3.18 Combination of accommodations
It may sometimes be necessary for an employer to take a combination of steps in order to accommodate a disabled employees needs fully. • Example: A worker who is blind is given a new job with her employer in an unfamiliar part of the building. The employer: o arranges facilities for her assistance dog in the new area. o arranges for her new instructions to be in Braille; and o provides disability equality training to all staff (EHRC 2011). In some cases, a reasonable adjustment will not succeed without the co-operation of other workers. Colleagues as well as managers may therefore have an important role in helping ensure that a reasonable adjustment is carried out in practice. Subject to considerations about confidentiality, employers must ensure that this happens. It is unlikely to be a valid defence to a claim under the Equality Act to argue that an adjustment was unreasonable because staff were obstructive or unhelpful when the employer tried to implement it. An employer would at least need to be able to show that they took such behaviour seriously and dealt with it appropriately. Employers will be more likely to be able to do this if they establish and implement policies and practices that promote equity, see our Working Practice Access Guidelines (Deane 2023e). • Example: An employer ensures that an autistic worker has a structured working day as a reasonable adjustment. As part of this adjustment, it is the responsibility of the employer to ensure that other workers co-operate with this arrangement (EHRC 2011). Page 26 of 30 4 How these guidelines were created

### 4.1 Mission
To remove the barriers to accessing life, so people can express their brilliance.

### 4.2 Our paradigms
We genuinely believe that anyone can work in science. We believe that having a diverse workforce enhances the quality and utility of the science created.

### 4.3 Key definitions
The core workplace of science is the laboratory. In these guidelines “Labs" refers to laboratories, manufacturing and production lines, engineering facilities, etc. “Scientists” refers to scientists, technologists, engineers, mathematicians, and healthcare professionals etc. “Disabled” relates to people who are disabled, D/deaf, or have long term health conditions (both physical and mental), illnesses, or injuries, that have a significant impact on their ability to carry out everyday tasks.

### 4.4 Aim
The aim was to create a set of documents that would provide a pragmatic and useful guide on to how to create an accessible lab workplace. We wished to accumulate relevant guidelines for lab contexts, edit them for relevancy, expand them in order to be as comprehensive as possible, and share them with the scientific community. The guidelines are mostly created from previously published work, which we cite. We wanted to provide guidelines for the whole of the lab work ecosystem, and to consider all types of impairments and disabilities. 1 Structural access – physical design of laboratory and fixed equipment (e.g., hoods, sinks etc.) 2 Equipment access – design and use of movable equipment (e.g., microscopes, centrifuges, PCR machines etc.) 3 Protocol access – adaptation of lab protocols to accommodate access needs (e.g., seated working, evacuation protocols, lone working etc.) 4 Dissemination access – work done in laboratories must be shared with the wider world. Access issues can be encountered in consultation and dissemination events, meetings, conferences, the publication of work on web pages and in journal articles. Page 27 of 30 5 General working practices access – adaptation of usual HR and working practices (e.g., part time or flexible hours), assisting disabled staff to access to relevant benefits, accessible transport and parking etc.

### 4.5 Team expertise
A significant proportion of the Access All Areas in Labs team have disabilities themselves, with lived experience of impairments in mobility, vision, stamina, dexterity, mental wellbeing, cognitive focus, and a range of neurodiversities. They have worked in microbiological, immunological, engineering, electronic, clinical trial, and pharmacy settings as students, researchers, principal investigators, technicians, and administrators.

### 4.6 Methods
We searched scientific databases (MEDLINE, EMBASE); grey literature; professional magazines; online resources; relevant charities and trade unions; centres for disability studies; consultants that support disabled researchers and employers. We snowballed contacts and resources from the originally identified literature. We also conducted a survey of people with an interest in lab access about barriers and solutions to lab access (Deane 2023d) along with a set of case study interviews examining solutions to lab access (AAAiLabs 2023). We identified a key guideline or two at the start of the creation of each of our guidelines. This would then be combined with information from other guidelines, data from the survey and case studies, and combined with the team’s lived expertise to allow us to provide comprehensive guidelines with exemplars of implementation solutions across a range of settings and impairments.

### 4.7 Amendments

sections.content: Page 1 of 39 Purpose of Guidelines These guidelines focus on the key accessibility considerations when disseminating the work conducted in a lab environment. This includes considerations about consultations, meetings, conferences, and public engagement events, whether in person, online, or hybrid in format. Disclaimer These guidelines are provided in good faith and are intended as an aid to good practice in accessibility. They cannot replace sound judgement, professional care, or common sense. They should be read and applied in conjunction with appropriate standards, and all relevant local regulations, codes of practice, and laws. Purpose of Guidelines

These guidelines focus on the key accessibility considerations when disseminating the work conducted in a lab environment. This includes considerations about consultations, meetings, conferences, and public engagement events, whether in person, online, or hybrid in format.

sections.heading: 1.1 Dissemination Access Principles
sections.content: Dissemination of the information created in laboratories requires accessible websites, consultation events, meetings, and conferences. We will discuss access in the context of online, in-person and hybrid information and events. 1 Organisations should ensure they celebrate diversity, and embed anti-ableist principles to ensure equity of access for disabled people (AIE 2020) a. When considering access to information and events the aim should be to have access solutions built-in and provided as a default. The aim should be to remove the need for a disabled person to have to request disability accommodations wherever possible. 2 All events must comply with the requirements of The Equality Act (2010) and make reasonable adjustments to operating practice that ensure disabled people are not unlawfully discriminated against (AIE 2020) 3 All actions relating to disabled people should be undertaken in accordance with the Social Model of Disability and aim to combat and eliminate ableism (AIE 2020) 4 Co-production with disabled people: disabled people should be consulted when organisations develop bespoke operating plans, and undertake Equality Impact Assessments before making decisions (AIE 2020) a. Respect participant’s needs and be open to accommodate other accessibility issues (WAI 2022) 5 The entire journey of attending your event for disabled people should be thoroughly mapped, ensuring it is equality impact assessed, clearly communicated in multiple formats (AIE 2020) a. Be aware of issues with • Vision • Hearing • Mobility • Speech • Understanding information presented in some ways well or at all • Mental wellbeing • Energy limitations • Dietary restrictions • Toileting needs Page 8 of 39 b. If you know there will be a barrier that cannot be avoided (e.g., steps, gravel paths, no hearing loop), or a service that cannot be provided (e.g., sign language interpretation) please state this clearly so as to avoid frustration and disappointment from participants.

sections.heading: 1.2 The social model of disability
sections.content: These guidelines are informed by the Social Model of Disability (Oliver 1990, Scope n.d.). This proposes that the majority of disability is caused by a lack of accommodation for impairments and differences. For example, a wheelchair user cannot get into a building because there are steps before the entrance. This is disabling not because the person is using a wheelchair but due to a lack of provision of a ramp. The responsibility for access lies with the owners of the building, not with the disabled person. “Barriers can make it impossible or very difficult to access jobs, buildings or services, but the biggest barrier of all is the problem of people’s attitude to disability. Removing the barriers is the best way to include millions of disabled people in our society” (TUC 2019).

sections.heading: 1.3 The duty to make reasonable adjustments
sections.source_heading: 1.3 The duty to make reasonable adjustments
sections.content: All employers have a legal duty under the Equality Act 2010 to proactively make reasonable adjustments to remove, reduce or prevent any disadvantages that disabled workers face (TUC 2019). In order to achieve equity for disabled people, work may need to be organised differently, support provided, and barriers removed.

sections.heading: 1.4 The benefits of accessible labs
sections.content: Labs are often designed without consideration to disability access due to the historic assumption that disabled scientists could not work safely in such environments. If disabled people’s needs are not designed into work and workplaces, then few disabled people will be able to work there. This is part of why there is a significant under representation of disabled people working in science, technology, engineering, and maths (STEM). Whilst approximately 22% of the UK adult population of working age are disabled, only around 3.8% of UK STEM academics are identified as disabled (Joice 2021). The lack of diversity in research participants and scientists is a factor in wasteful research due to serious flaws in prioritisation, design, sampling, analysis and interpretation, etc. (Glasziou 2018; Macleod 2014; JLA 2023). Research that is informed by a diverse multidisciplinary team is better able to ensure practicality, utility, and impact (Deane 2014 and 2019, Schroeder 2022). The opportunity cost of not having disabled scientists with their diversity of experience and expertise is likely to be significant. Additionally, most disabilities are acquired; the loss of highly qualified scientists from the field when they acquire a disability is a substantial loss on the investment in their training. We start with the assumption that all disabled scientists are able to work in labs, if the labs are designed with their access needs met. Safety issues can be designed “out” of the labs; Page 9 of 39 either in the structural or equipment design or in the protocols used. Accessibility also includes the design of the work processes, staff knowledge and attitudes. Accessible labs will allow a greater proportion of disabled scientists to be trained and work in lab settings in a safe and comfortable manner. We genuinely believe this improved diversity in the workforce will enhance the quality and potential profitability of the work done in laboratory settings. Page 10 of 39

sections.content: • Embrace the all-access attitude. • You have to test for accessibility with real users. • Accessibility is cheaper when it’s done up front. (Mortensen 2023).

sections.content: • Prioritise visual access; covers 80% of web accessibility issues. • Ideally text size and contrast should be changeable. • Remember to create good ALT text (text that describes images). • Videos should have closed caption options. sections.heading: 2.3 Event access
sections.content: • Plan ahead for access, including a budget. • Make it explicit that you welcome disabled people to your event o Ask about access needs prominently, but keep disclosures confidential. o Provide detailed information about access accommodations. • Virtual or hybrid events need to particularly consider visual and hearing access. o Auto transcription should always be an option that can be selected. o Consideration should be given to providing sign language interpretation, audio description, and note takers (see section 5.1). • Remember that speakers may be disabled, as well as audience members. • Train your staff and provide information to speakers about expected standards of behaviour to promote access. • Everyone uses a microphone in group events (speakers and audience). • Consider the whole journey of accessing the event; transport, accommodation etc. • Quiet rooms are incredibly helpful for many disabilities. • Assistance dogs must be admitted and having water and spend pounds is helpful. • Carer tickets should be free. sections.content: Documents may be produced for hard copy or for electronic format. Documents that are placed on web pages should follow the advice in section 4.

sections.heading: 3.1 Keep the language simple
sections.content: Use clear simple language. This particularly helps those with cognitive impairments and learning disabilities. However, this helps everyone understand and process the information quickly (GOV.UK 2020). There you need to use technical terms, abbreviations or acronyms, explain what they mean the first time you use them (GOV.UK 2020)

sections.heading: 3.2 Easy Read Format
sections.content: You should consider making your documents default to an easy read format. If you don’t do this, you should consider providing an easy read version of your documents. In general, the following recommendations should be followed: Text should be broken down into short sentences. Images should be selected to represent each sentence of text where possible. Language should be simplified wherever possible, and any necessary complicated words or terms should be explained. Avoid fancy fonts and italics. Design elements should be kept to a minimum to stop them detracting from the information. (FPLD 2023).

sections.heading: 3.3 Text Format
sections.content: Use sans serif fonts, e.g. Arial, Comic Sans, Verdana, Tahoma, Century Gothic, Trebuchet, Calibri, Open Sans. Try not to use serif or ‘handwritten’ fonts or capital letters for long, continuous blocks of text – they are hard to read. Avoid underlining and italics, as this can make the text appear to run together and causes crowding. If further emphasis is required, use bold. Avoid continuous uppercase or capital letter text (NTR 2019). Font size: 12pt is the absolute minimum. 14pt is best. For headings, use a font size that is at least 20% larger than the normal text (GOV.UK 2020; NTR 2019). Larger inter-letter / character spacing (sometimes called tracking) improves readability. (In MS Word: Home - Font – Expand – Advanced – Spacing – Expanded – 0.8pt). Larger line spacing improves readability and should be proportional to inter-word spacing; 1.5 / 150% is preferable. Add extra space around headings and between paragraphs (NTR 2019).

sections.heading: 3.4 Design and Production
sections.content: Keep designs clear, simple and clutter-free. (‘White space’ is great.) Page 12 of 39 Left align text, without justification. Avoid multiple columns (as used in newspapers). Lines should not be too long: 60 to 70 characters. Break up the text with regular section headings in long documents and include a table of contents. Images support meaning when chosen well. Illustrate your commitment to equality with images that include disabled people and show off your access provisions. All images should have a brief description underneath them, for visually impaired people using text readers. Do not put text over images. Where possible, or when the document will be in circulation for the publication for long periods of time, create an EasyRead version of the document, to make the information accessible to people with Learning Disabilities. Offer multiple formats of the information. Provide an option for the document in Word/Plain Text format and PDF format, this allows people to choose how they interact with the information. Consider providing brief videos of the text being read out. Consider providing BSL videos of text. Consider Sign-A-Long or Makaton videos of text for information relevant to communities that use these forms of communication. Always include information about disabled access within any space where an event is taking place (e.g. level access, lifts, toilets, hearing loops etc.) See Section 5 Event access for more information.

sections.heading: 3.5 Writing Style
sections.content: Use active rather than passive voice. Be concise; avoid using long, dense paragraphs. Use short, simple sentences in a direct style. Use images to support text. Flow charts are ideal for explaining procedures. Pictograms and graphics can help to locate and support information in the text. Consider bullet points & numbering rather than continuous prose. Give instructions clearly. Avoid double negatives. Avoid abbreviations where possible; always provide the expanded form when first used. Provide a glossary of abbreviations and jargon.

sections.heading: 3.6 Colour
sections.content: Use single colour backgrounds. Avoid background patterns or pictures and distracting surrounds. Use sufficient contrast levels between background and text. Use dark coloured text on a light background. Avoid green and red/pink, as these colours are difficult for those who have colour blindness. Consider alternatives to white backgrounds for paper, computer and visual aids such as whiteboards. White can appear too dazzling. Use cream or a soft pastel colour. Some dyslexic people will have their own colour preference. Page 13 of 39 With long documents, offer the document as a word file, electronically, so that readers can determine their own colour, size, spacing and contrast preferences. For colour blindness it is best to avoid these colour combinations (Collinge 2017): • Green and Red • Green and Brown • Blue and Purple • Green and Blue • Light Green and Yellow • Blue and Grey • Green and Grey • Green and Black Other colour combinations that can be difficult: • Yellow and Purple • White writing on bright backgrounds • White writing on pale backgrounds Photoshop can simulate the experience of viewing a document with colour blindness with these two proofing commands: View > Proof Setup > Color Blindness - Protanopia Type View > Proof Setup > Color Blindness - Deuteranopia Type

sections.heading: 4 Web page and electronic document access

sections.heading: 4.1 W3C WAI Web accessibility standards (2019)
sections.parent_heading: 4 Web page and electronic document access
sections.content: This is a summary, further details of examples, standards, and implementation guidance is available from the W3C WAI web pages. Web accessibility relies on several components that work together. Some of these include: Web content - refers to any part of a website, including text, images, forms, and multimedia, as well as any markup code, scripts, applications, and such. User agents - software that people use to access web content, including desktop graphical browsers, voice browsers, mobile phone browsers, multimedia players, plug-ins, and some assistive technologies. Authoring tools - software or services that people use to produce web content, including code editors, document conversion tools, content management systems, blogs, database scripts, and other tools.

sections.heading: 4.2.4 Content is easier to see and hear Distinguishable content is easier to see and hear. Such content includes:
sections.content: • Colour is not used as the only way of conveying information or identifying content • Default foreground and background colour combinations provide sufficient contrast • When users resize text up to 400% or change text spacing, no information is lost • Text reflows in small windows (“viewports”) and when users make the text larger • Images of text are resizable, replaced with actual text, or avoided where possible • Users can pause, stop, or adjust the volume of audio that is played on a website • Background audio is low or can be turned off, to avoid interference or distraction

sections.heading: 4.3.1 Functionality is available from a keyboard
sections.source_heading: 4.3.1 Functionality is available from a keyboard
sections.content: Many people do not use the mouse and rely on the keyboard to interact with the Web. This requires keyboard access to all functionality, including form controls, input, and other user interface components. Keyboard accessibility includes: • All functionality that is available by mouse is also available by keyboard • Keyboard focus does not get trapped in any part of the content • Web browsers, authoring tools, and other tools provide keyboard support

sections.heading: 4.3.2 Users have enough time to read and use the content
sections.source_heading: 4.3.2 Users have enough time to read and use the content
sections.content: Some people need more time than others to read and use the content. For instance, some people require more time to type text, understand instructions, operate controls, or to otherwise complete tasks on a website. Examples of providing enough time include providing mechanisms to: • Stop, extend, or adjust time limits, except where necessary • Pause, stop, or hide moving, blinking, or scrolling content • Postpone or suppress interruptions, except where necessary • Re-authenticate when a session expires without losing data

sections.heading: 4.3.3 Content does not cause seizures and physical reactions
sections.source_heading: 4.3.3 Content does not cause seizures and physical reactions
sections.content: Content that flashes at certain rates or patterns can cause photosensitive reactions, including seizures. Flashing content is ideally avoided entirely or only used in a way that Page 16 of 39 does not cause known risks. Also, animations and moving content can cause discomfort and physical reactions. Examples of avoiding causing seizures and physical reactions: • Do not include content that flashes at particular rates and patterns • Warn users before flashing content is presented, and provide alternatives • Provide mechanisms to switch off animations, unless they are essential

sections.heading: 4.3.4 Users can easily navigate, find content, and determine where they are
sections.source_heading: 4.3.4 Users can easily navigate, find content, and determine where they are
sections.content: Well organized content helps users to orient themselves and to navigate effectively. Such content includes: • Pages have clear titles and are organized using descriptive section headings • There is more than one way to find relevant pages within a set of web pages • Users are informed about their current location within a set of related pages • There are ways to bypass blocks of content that are repeated on multiple pages • The keyboard focus is visible, and the focus order follows a meaningful sequence • The purpose of a link is evident, ideally even when the link is viewed on its own

sections.heading: 4.3.5 Users can use different input modalities beyond keyboard
sections.source_heading: 4.3.5 Users can use different input modalities beyond keyboard
sections.content: Input modalities beyond keyboard, such as touch activation, voice recognition (speech input), and gestures make content easier to use for many people. Yet not everyone can use each of these input modalities, and to the same degree. Particular design considerations maximize the benefit of these input modalities. This includes: • Gestures that require dexterity or fine movement have alternatives that do not require high dexterity • Components are designed to avoid accidental activation, for example by providing undo functionality • Labels presented to users match corresponding object names in the code, to support activation by voice • Functionality that is activated by movement can also be activated through user interface components • Buttons, links, and other active components are large enough to make them easier to activate by touch Understandable information and user interface 4.3.6 Text is readable and understandable Content authors need to ensure that text content is readable and understandable to the broadest audience possible, including when it is read aloud by text-to-speech. Such content includes: Page 17 of 39 • Identifying the primary language of a web page, such as Arabic, Dutch, or Korean • Identifying the language of text passages, phrases, or other parts of a web page • Providing definitions for any unusual words, phrases, idioms, and abbreviations • Using the clearest and simplest language possible, or providing simplified versions • Consider providing Plain Language Summaries or Easy Read options (FPLD 2023)

sections.heading: 4.3.7 Content appears and operates in predictable ways
sections.content: Many people rely on predictable user interfaces and are disoriented or distracted by inconsistent appearance or behaviour. 6 Event Access

sections.heading: 6.1 Planning the Event
sections.parent_heading: 4 Web page and electronic document access
sections.content: • Finding an accessible venue. Websites such as Euan’s Guide (https://www.euansguide.com/) and DisabledGo (https://www.accessable.co.uk/), or the Snowball access app (available from Google Play and the App Store) can help identify potential venues in your area. You must visit the venue and check all issues to ensure your meeting or event is accessible – do not trust the venue’s reports on access – they can be “optimistic”. • Ensure that promotional and registration information is available in a variety of formats including electronic format (ADCET 2017). • Ensure that participants are provided with multiple options for registration including phone, email, and online. Ensure that online forms are accessible to screen readers (ADCET 2017). • At the time of registration, ask about any accessibility requirements that participants may have (ADCET 2017). • Ensure that registration is available at no charge for carers (ADCET 2017). • Take care to ensure all the tools used in an online environment ensure access for all participants. For example, white board software which allow participants to contribute comments may not be compatible with screen readers. • Sign Language interpreters should be provided as a default for larger events and must be provided anytime sign language interpretation is requested. For British Sign Language interpreters should be above Level 4 in skill and on one of the following registers: The National Registers of Communication Professionals working with Deaf and Deafblind People (NRCPD), The Regulatory Body for Sign Language Interpreters and Translators (RBSLI), or the Scottish Register of Language Professionals with the Deaf Community (SRLPDC). • Scripts of pre-prepared talks should be provided to the sign language interpreters sufficiently in advance to allow them to prepare. This is particularly important if you will be using technical terms. • Consideration should be given to providing live captioning. Whilst auto-generated closed captions are now available for video calling software packages their accuracy can be poor for technical topics.

Websites such as Euan’s Guide (https://www.euansguide.com/) and DisabledGo (https://www.accessable.co.uk/), or the Snowball access app (available from Google Play and the App Store) can help identify potential venues in your area. You must visit the venue and check all issues to ensure your meeting or event is accessible – do not trust the venue’s reports on access – they can be “optimistic”. • Ensure that promotional and registration information is available in a variety of formats including electronic format (ADCET 2017). • Ensure that participants are provided with multiple options for registration including phone, email, and online. Ensure that online forms are accessible to screen readers (ADCET 2017). • At the time of registration, ask about any accessibility requirements that participants may have (ADCET 2017). • Ensure that registration is available at no charge for carers (ADCET 2017). • Take care to ensure all the tools used in an online environment ensure access for all participants. sections.heading: 6.1.1 Check venue access Ensure that the planned location for the event is accessible. Check the following:
sections.content: • Is it close to public transport or car parking or is there a drop off point? (ADCET 2017) • Is there a clear path of travel to the building? Is it well signposted? Easy entry? Automatic doors? (ADCET 2017) Page 23 of 39 • Does it have step free access – to meeting room, the stage, accessible toilets, quiet room, breakout rooms, dining areas, poster rooms? (Thresholds should not be greater than 3cm high). • Are there stairs and if so, do they have handrails? Is there an accessible lift as an alternative to the stairs? (ADCET 2017) • Does the venue have sufficient space? Wheelchair users need space. Always provide generous turning circles etc, as tight spaces mean damage e.g., to doorways and wheelchairs. Additionally, whilst a single wheelchair user will usually take up “2 people spaces”, when two wheelchair users are in a single space they will need around “6 people spaces” in order to circulate freely. • Is there a hearing loop or similar hearing technology? If none is available, consider providing a portable hearing loop. • Are accessible bathroom facilities in close proximity to the venue? (ADCET 2017). And that they are of an appropriate size (EDF 2019) with suitable size bins for incontinence pads. • Are the accessible toilets free of clutter e.g., cleaning materials, spare chairs, etc. • Are there Changing Place accessible toilets (with hoist and bench) available at or near the venue. (Such facilities can be found at https://www.changingplaces.org/find). If a Changing Place accessible toilet is not available close to the venue consideration should be given to the hire of portable facilities e.g. https://www.mobiloo.org.uk is a Changing Place in the back of a van that can be parked by your venue. • Is there a quiet space available? (ADCET 2017) This is a room separate to the rest of the event, with chairs, and ideally a bench, cushions, and adjustable lighting. • Is there a place for assistance animals to rest, be toileted and watered? (ADCET 2017) • Does the venue have good ventilation target CO2 concentrations below 800ppm or typically 10 l/s/person (CIBSE 2021).
