sections.heading: 6.1.2 Training Volunteers and Event Managers
sections.content: Train your team to be confident asking people with visible disabilities if they need assistance – and to listen to the answer. The team need to know where the accessible toilet is, the best place to sit to have good lines of sight for lip readers or wheelchair users, the fire evacuation routes, how to work the lift etc. The team need to have knowledge of where access equipment is kept e.g., mobile hearing loop, or the Radar key for the accessible toilet, or the code for the platform lift etc. They should know who to contact in the event of equipment or facilities developing a fault. Purple Reach can provide disability awareness and equality training https://www.purplereach.co.uk/. Your team should know that assistance dogs have a legal right to access all venues and how to interact with them. Page 24 of 39 (https://www.guidedog.org/PuppyRaising/PuppyRaiserManual/Resources/Assistance_Dog_ Etiquette.aspx). Ideally teach your team a few British Sign Language signs e.g., hello, welcome, thank you, sorry, and drink? (https://actiononhearingloss.org.uk/wpcontent/uploads/2020/05/Learning-British-Sign-Language-leaflet.pdf). Your team should be confident in prioritising the needs of those with disabilities i.e., asking audience members to move seats to allow better access for someone in a wheelchair or who needs to be close to the presenter to lip read or use the portable hearing loop. Do your team know how to respond to first aid issues when associated with disability? E.g., responding appropriately to an epileptic fit (https://www.epilepsy.org.uk/info/firstaid). Do your team know how to assist in the evacuation of a disabled person? Further information on such fire evacuation protocols are described in the Protocol Access Guidelines (Deane 2023b)

sections.heading: 6.1.3 Speaker Preparation
sections.content: You also need to prepare your speakers. If you are using sign language interpreters, ask that they provide a script of their talk at least a week in advance to allow the interpreters to prepare. Let them know that you expect a diverse audience. Speakers should be asked to use a microphone (if available) for all of their talk – irrespective of their vocal volume – as amplified speech is easier for hearing aids to pick up, and easier to feed into hybrid meetings. They should consider this when asking for audience participation e.g., a Deaf person invited to participate may need a friend to do BSL interpretation for them; not everyone may be able to “stand up and take part” in an activity. Also, audience members may be more “distracting” than usual, e.g., vocal outbursts from someone with Tourette’s, or stimming (e.g., flapping hands, or rocking back and forth) for autistic people. Obviously, you need to ask your speaker to be accommodating of these differences.

sections.heading: 6.2 Prior to Event
sections.parent_heading: 4 Web page and electronic document access
sections.content: Ensure that all requested accessibility requirements are arranged. This may include the following: • Arranging sign language interpreters (ADCET 2017). • Arranging for any video material to be captioned (ADCET 2017). • Arranging for live captioning services (ADCET 2017). • Provision of written material in an appropriately accessible format prior to the event (ADCET 2017) i.e., black text on pastel coloured paper, sans serif font, left justified. 12 points for standard text and 16 points for enlarged text formats. Repeat for electronic documents and provide both word and pdf formats. Page 25 of 39 • Ensure that participants are provided with accessible maps in an appropriate format. This may include visual, text and audio maps (ADCET 2017). • Check access equipment is in working order e.g., lifts, stair lifts, hearing loops etc. Ensure the venue knows they must contact you urgently if any of these facilities fail prior to the event. Have a communications plan to contact attendees who need these facilities as soon as possible and offer full refunds if access cannot be guaranteed. • Check the red cord alarms in the accessible toilets work, that they will be responded to promptly, and that they are not tied up. Red cord cards are highly effective in preventing cords being tied up https://www.euansguide.com/news/red-cord-card/. • • FIGURE 1 A picture of Euan’s Guide’s Red Cord Card • Check accessible evacuation routes and whether personal emergency evacuation plans (PEEPs) should be created. There may be a maximum number of wheelchair users or mobility impaired people allowed in a given space.

sections.heading: 6.3 On the day of the event
sections.parent_heading: 4 Web page and electronic document access
sections.content: Ensure that venue, facilities, and event signage is: • Clear (ADCET 2017). Uses text and pictograms where appropriate. • Utilises accessible contrast (ADCET 2017). Page 26 of 39 • Is at an appropriate height to be seen (ADCET 2017) i.e., 700-1000mm above floor level (Building Regulations 2010). • Includes raised tactile and/ or braille information where required (e.g., on doors and bathrooms) (ADCET 2017). Ensure that participants are provided with accessible maps in an appropriate format, which indicate the location of event venues and accessible facilities (ADCET 2017). Ensure that access to and location of venue facilities is communicated to participants. This might include: • The presence of a hearing induction loop or infrared hearing assistance system (ADCET 2017). • The location of accessible bathroom facilities (ADCET 2017). • The location of assistance animal rest areas (ADCET 2017). • The location of quiet spaces (ADCET 2017). Ensure that clear paths of travel are provided both outside and within the venue. The venue and environs should be clear of obstacles and trip hazards such as electrical cables should be moved or taped down (ADCET 2017). Ensure that the venue is well lit throughout, and that glare is minimised. (ADCET 2017). Ensure the venue has good temperature control which can be adjusted according to need. Provision of hot or cold drinks can also aid a disabled person’s ability to regulate their temperature. Ensure the venue is well ventilated and will maintain a good standard of ventilation with the number of attendees planned i.e., target CO2 concentrations below 800ppm or typically 10 l/s/person (CIBSE 2021). Face masks are effective at preventing the spread of respiratory infections such as COVID-19 (Cheng 2021). Many disabled people are at disproportionately high risk from such infections therefore having a policy of proactively supporting them is helpful. You can do this by specifically asking about this issue at registration. If you do have someone attending who is at high risk, you should let everyone else attending know this (but obviously do not name the delegate), and strongly encouraging everyone (except for those who are medically exempt), to wear masks. However, we do recognise that face masks can reduce ease of communication for people who are hard of hearing and who lip read. In these instances, removing the face mask whilst speaking is acceptable. For outdoor events, ensure that shaded areas are provided for people who are sensitive to heat or who experience light or glare sensitivity. (ADCET 2017). Ensure that the registration table is at an appropriate height for all participants including wheelchair users and people of short stature. (ADCET 2017). Page 27 of 39 Ensure all speakers are required to use the microphone. Roving audience microphones are provided where audience participation is anticipated. (ADCET 2017). Lapel microphones or adjustable height microphones should be used to accommodate people at different heights. (ADCET 2017). Ensure that the presenters and any participants who need to, can access the stage or equivalent (ADCET 2017). Ramps to the stage should not exceed 1:10 slope and should be at least 900mm wide. Ensure that there is an emergency plan for the event, that staff are aware of the plan and that emergency procedures address how people with disability will be assisted. (ADCET 2017).

sections.heading: 6.3.1 For events providing refreshments and food
sections.parent_heading: 6.3 On the day of the event
sections.content: Ensure that buffet lunch tables are at an appropriate height for all participants including wheelchair users and people of short stature. (ADCET 2017). Ensure that food for people with allergies, intolerances etc can be served up separately from the buffet to prevent cross-contamination. Food should be well labelled, and staff should be able to access detailed information on allergens etc. Can the venue provide facilities to warm pureed food? (Some disabled people have very restricted dietary options and can only eat pureed food). Ensure the venue will provide straws for customers on request? Ensure there are servers available to assist with buffets, to carry food to tables etc. Ensure that there are tables at an appropriate height for wheelchair users to put food and drinks on. Ensure that there is a lowered counter to allow payments. Ensure card readers have sufficiently long cables to allow easy reach from a chair or by people of restricted growth.

sections.heading: 6.3.4 For standing events
sections.parent_heading: 6.3 On the day of the event
sections.content: Provide some chairs for people who may not be able to stand for extended periods or who may experience fatigue. (ADCET 2017). For both of the above, ensure that some seating with arms is available. (ADCET 2017). 6.3.5 For online or hybrid events Online or hybrid events can create improved disability access by removing the risk of infection, reducing the energy required to participate, and removing the challenge of travelling to the venue. However these types of events do bring their own access challenges that must be accommodated. • Ensure you have a chairperson and someone else to manage the chat and solve technical difficulties. • For events with more than about 10 participants it is usual best to turn off video and sound for participants unless they are speaking to ensure good call quality for everyone, including those with low bandwidth. • Ask those speaking to be well lit and close to their camera to ensure those who lip read can see their faces. • Ask presenters to introduce themselves with a brief visual description of themselves e.g. “I am a white woman, with short brown hair, wearing a blue floral dress.” • Those presenting should be aware of the need to provide a clear description of visual information such as graphs. • Participants must be able to “pin” the picture with the BSL interpreter alongside the main presentation. Note that with longer events you may have more than one interpreter, in more than one location, who need to swap in and out smoothly. Look at how you are going to ensure this change-over happens seamlessly for the audience. If you split into virtual breakout rooms, ensure the BSL interpreter will be in the same room as the Deaf person(s). • If the event is hybrid, it is best practice to have one person to focus on the online participants and another on the in-person participants.

For both of the above, ensure that some seating with arms is available. (ADCET 2017). 6.3.5 For online or hybrid events

Online or hybrid events can create improved disability access by removing the risk of infection, reducing the energy required to participate, and removing the challenge of travelling to the venue. However these types of events do bring their own access challenges that must be accommodated.

Ensure you have a chairperson and someone else to manage the chat and solve technical difficulties. • For events with more than about 10 participants it is usual best to turn off video and sound for participants unless they are speaking to ensure good call quality for everyone, including those with low bandwidth. • Ask those speaking to be well lit and close to their camera to ensure those who lip read can see their faces. • Ask presenters to introduce themselves with a brief visual description of themselves e.g. “I am a white woman, with short brown hair, wearing a blue floral dress.” • Those presenting should be aware of the need to provide a clear description of visual information such as graphs. • Participants must be able to “pin” the picture with the BSL interpreter alongside the main presentation. Note that with longer events you may have more than one interpreter, in more than one location, who need to swap in and out smoothly. Look at how you are going to ensure this change-over happens seamlessly for the audience. If you split into virtual breakout rooms, ensure the BSL interpreter will be in the same room as the Deaf person(s). • If the event is hybrid, it is best practice to have one person to focus on the online participants and another on the in-person participants.

sections.heading: 9.3 Key definitions
sections.parent_heading: 4 Web page and electronic document access
sections.content: The core workplace of science is the laboratory. In these guidelines “Labs" refers to laboratories, manufacturing and production lines, engineering facilities, etc. “Scientists” refers to scientists, technologists, engineers, mathematicians, and healthcare professionals etc. “Disabled” relates to people who are disabled, D/deaf, or have long term health conditions (both physical and mental), illnesses, or injuries, which have a significant impact on their ability to carry out everyday tasks.

sections.heading: 9.4 Aim
sections.parent_heading: 4 Web page and electronic document access
sections.content: The aim was to create a set of documents that would provide a pragmatic and useful guide on to how to create an accessible lab workplace. We wished to accumulate relevant guidelines for lab contexts, edit them for relevancy, expand them in order to be as 8omprehensive as possible, and share them with the scientific community. The guidelines are mostly created from previously published work, which we cite. We wanted to provide guidelines for the whole of the lab work ecosystem, and to consider all types of impairments and disabilities. 1 Structural access – physical design of laboratory and fixed equipment (e.g., hoods, sinks etc.) 2 Equipment access – design and use of movable equipment (e.g., microscopes, centrifuges, PCR machines etc.) 3 Protocol access – adaptation of lab protocols to accommodate access needs (e.g., seated working, evacuation protocols, lone working etc.) 4 Dissemination access – work done in laboratories must be shared with the wider world. Access issues can be encountered in consultation and dissemination events, meetings, conferences, the publication of work on web pages and in journal articles. Page 36 of 39 5 General working practices access – adaptation of usual HR and working practices (e.g., part time or flexible hours), assisting disabled staff to access to relevant benefits, accessible transport and parking etc.

sections.heading: 9.5 Team expertise
sections.parent_heading: 4 Web page and electronic document access
sections.content: A significant proportion of the Access All Areas in Labs team have disabilities themselves, with lived experience of impairments in mobility, vision, stamina, dexterity, mental wellbeing, cognitive focus, and a range of neurodiversities. They have worked in microbiological, immunological, engineering, electronic, clinical trial, and pharmacy settings as students, researchers, principal investigators, technicians, and administrators.

sections.heading: 9.6 Methods
sections.parent_heading: 4 Web page and electronic document access
sections.content: We searched scientific databases (MEDLINE, EMBASE); grey literature; professional magazines; online resources; relevant charities and trade unions; centres for disability studies; consultants that support disabled researchers and employers. We snowballed contacts and resources from the originally identified literature. We also conducted a survey of people with an interest in lab access about barriers and solutions to lab access (Deane 2023a) along with a set of case study interviews examining solutions to lab access (AAAiLabs 2023). We identified a key guideline or two at the start of the creation of each of our guidelines. This would then be combined with information from other guidelines, data from the survey and case studies, and combined with the team’s lived expertise to allow us to provide comprehensive guidelines with exemplars of implementation solutions across a range of settings and impairments.

extracted.body_text: Page 1 of 39 Purpose of Guidelines These guidelines focus on the key accessibility considerations when disseminating the work conducted in a lab environment. This includes considerations about consultations, meetings, conferences, and public engagement events, whether in person, online, or hybrid in format. Disclaimer These guidelines are provided in good faith and are intended as an aid to good practice in accessibility. They cannot replace sound judgement, professional care, or common sense. They should be read and applied in conjunction with appropriate standards, and all relevant local regulations, codes of practice, and laws. These guidelines constitute a live document and may be subject to change in the future where the authors consider it appropriate in the light of new information or developments in the field of accessibility. Comments and Corrections We welcome comments and corrections on these guidelines that will allow us to enhance the next version’s quality and relevancy. If you have suggestions for changes, please email Dr Katherine Deane k.deane@uea.ac.uk Acknowledgements These guidelines were created by the Access All Areas in Labs team which included: • Katherine Deane, Associate Professor and Access Ambassador, University of East Anglia, k.deane@uea.ac.uk • Thomas Fadden, Purple Reach Disability Access Consultancy, tom@purplereach.co.uk • Jenny Camaradou, Independent Expert on Knowledge Exchange, Grant Writing, and Patient Engagement, jenny@healthclusternet.eu • Peter Hemmins, Senior Lab Technician, Productivity East, Science Faculty University of East Anglia • Dan Burrill, Lab Technician, Science Faculty, University of East Anglia Funding This project was funded by a grant award from Innovate UK to the Cell & Gene Therapy Catapult. Additionally Katherine Deane, UEA, is supported by the National Institute for Health and Care Research (NIHR) Applied Research Collaboration East of England (NIHR ARC EoE) at Cambridge and Peterborough NHS Foundation Trust. The views expressed are those Page 2 of 39 of the author[s] and not necessarily those of the NIHR or the Department of Health and Social Care. About the Cell and Gene Therapy Catapult The Cell and Gene Therapy Catapult is an independent innovation and technology organisation committed to the advancement of cell and gene therapies with a vision of a thriving industry delivering life changing advanced therapies to the world. Its aim is to create powerful collaborations which overcome challenges to the advancement of the sector. With over 400 experts covering all aspects of advanced therapies, it applies its unique capabilities and assets, collaborates with academia, industry and healthcare providers to develop new technology and innovation. The Cell and Gene Therapy Catapult works with Innovate UK. For more information, please visit https://ct.catapult.org.uk/ or http://www.gov.uk/innovate-uk. .......................................................................................................................... 38 Page 7 of 39 Dissemination of the information created in laboratories requires accessible websites, consultation events, meetings, and conferences. We will discuss access in the context of online, in-person and hybrid information and events. 1 Organisations should ensure they celebrate diversity, and embed anti-ableist principles to ensure equity of access for disabled people (AIE 2020) a. When considering access to information and events the aim should be to have access solutions built-in and provided as a default. The aim should be to remove the need for a disabled person to have to request disability accommodations wherever possible. 2 All events must comply with the requirements of The Equality Act (2010) and make reasonable adjustments to operating practice that ensure disabled people are not unlawfully discriminated against (AIE 2020) 3 All actions relating to disabled people should be undertaken in accordance with the Social Model of Disability and aim to combat and eliminate ableism (AIE 2020) 4 Co-production with disabled people: disabled people should be consulted when organisations develop bespoke operating plans, and undertake Equality Impact Assessments before making decisions (AIE 2020) a. Respect participant’s needs and be open to accommodate other accessibility issues (WAI 2022) 5 The entire journey of attending your event for disabled people should be thoroughly mapped, ensuring it is equality impact assessed, clearly communicated in multiple formats (AIE 2020) a. Be aware of issues with • Vision • Hearing • Mobility • Speech • Understanding information presented in some ways well or at all • Mental wellbeing • Energy limitations • Dietary restrictions • Toileting needs Page 8 of 39 b. If you know there will be a barrier that cannot be avoided (e.g., steps, gravel paths, no hearing loop), or a service that cannot be provided (e.g., sign language interpretation) please state this clearly so as to avoid frustration and disappointment from participants. These guidelines are informed by the Social Model of Disability (Oliver 1990, Scope n.d.). This proposes that the majority of disability is caused by a lack of accommodation for impairments and differences. For example, a wheelchair user cannot get into a building because there are steps before the entrance. This is disabling not because the person is using a wheelchair but due to a lack of provision of a ramp. The responsibility for access lies with the owners of the building, not with the disabled person. “Barriers can make it impossible or very difficult to access jobs, buildings or services, but the biggest barrier of all is the problem of people’s attitude to disability. Removing the barriers is the best way to include millions of disabled people in our society” (TUC 2019). All employers have a legal duty under the Equality Act 2010 to proactively make reasonable adjustments to remove, reduce or prevent any disadvantages that disabled workers face (TUC 2019). In order to achieve equity for disabled people, work may need to be organised differently, support provided, and barriers removed. Labs are often designed without consideration to disability access due to the historic assumption that disabled scientists could not work safely in such environments. If disabled people’s needs are not designed into work and workplaces, then few disabled people will be able to work there. This is part of why there is a significant under representation of disabled people working in science, technology, engineering, and maths (STEM). Whilst approximately 22% of the UK adult population of working age are disabled, only around 3.8% of UK STEM academics are identified as disabled (Joice 2021). The lack of diversity in research participants and scientists is a factor in wasteful research due to serious flaws in prioritisation, design, sampling, analysis and interpretation, etc. (Glasziou 2018; Macleod 2014; JLA 2023). Research that is informed by a diverse multidisciplinary team is better able to ensure practicality, utility, and impact (Deane 2014 and 2019, Schroeder 2022). The opportunity cost of not having disabled scientists with their diversity of experience and expertise is likely to be significant. Additionally, most disabilities are acquired; the loss of highly qualified scientists from the field when they acquire a disability is a substantial loss on the investment in their training. We start with the assumption that all disabled scientists are able to work in labs, if the labs are designed with their access needs met. Safety issues can be designed “out” of the labs; Page 9 of 39 either in the structural or equipment design or in the protocols used. Accessibility also includes the design of the work processes, staff knowledge and attitudes. Accessible labs will allow a greater proportion of disabled scientists to be trained and work in lab settings in a safe and comfortable manner. We genuinely believe this improved diversity in the workforce will enhance the quality and potential profitability of the work done in laboratory settings. Page 10 of 39 • Embrace the all-access attitude. • You have to test for accessibility with real users. • Accessibility is cheaper when it’s done up front. (Mortensen 2023). • Simple text, short sentences, with use of images to aid comprehension (FPLD 2023) • Text should be provided in a sans serif font, at least 12 point size, left aligned, 1.5 line spacing, on a pastel coloured background. • Large print versions (at lest 16 point size) should be available. • Text should have a plain background (don’t place text over pictures) (NTR 2019). • Prioritise visual access; covers 80% of web accessibility issues. • Ideally text size and contrast should be changeable. • Remember to create good ALT text (text that describes images). • Videos should have closed caption options. Consideration should be given to sign language interpretation and audio description of videos (see section 5.1). • Don’t place important content out of the way where screen readers won’t find it. • Check mobile and screen reader accessibility separately. • Don’t disable zoom in mobile interfaces. (Mortensen 2023). • Plan ahead for access, including a budget. • Make it explicit that you welcome disabled people to your event o Ask about access needs prominently, but keep disclosures confidential. o Provide detailed information about access accommodations. • Virtual or hybrid events need to particularly consider visual and hearing access. o Auto transcription should always be an option that can be selected. o Consideration should be given to providing sign language interpretation, audio description, and note takers (see section 5.1). • Remember that speakers may be disabled, as well as audience members. • Train your staff and provide information to speakers about expected standards of behaviour to promote access. • Everyone uses a microphone in group events (speakers and audience). • Consider the whole journey of accessing the event; transport, accommodation etc. • Quiet rooms are incredibly helpful for many disabilities. • Assistance dogs must be admitted and having water and spend pounds is helpful. • Carer tickets should be free. The proofs needed to access these should be simple. Page 11 of 39 Documents may be produced for hard copy or for electronic format. Documents that are placed on web pages should follow the advice in section 4. Use clear simple language. This particularly helps those with cognitive impairments and learning disabilities. However, this helps everyone understand and process the information quickly (GOV.UK 2020). There you need to use technical terms, abbreviations or acronyms, explain what they mean the first time you use them (GOV.UK 2020) You should consider making your documents default to an easy read format. If you don’t do this, you should consider providing an easy read version of your documents. In general, the following recommendations should be followed: Text should be broken down into short sentences. Images should be selected to represent each sentence of text where possible. Language should be simplified wherever possible, and any necessary complicated words or terms should be explained. Avoid fancy fonts and italics. Design elements should be kept to a minimum to stop them detracting from the information. (FPLD 2023). Use sans serif fonts, e.g. Arial, Comic Sans, Verdana, Tahoma, Century Gothic, Trebuchet, Calibri, Open Sans. Try not to use serif or ‘handwritten’ fonts or capital letters for long, continuous blocks of text – they are hard to read. Avoid underlining and italics, as this can make the text appear to run together and causes crowding. If further emphasis is required, use bold. Avoid continuous uppercase or capital letter text (NTR 2019). Font size: 12pt is the absolute minimum. 14pt is best. For headings, use a font size that is at least 20% larger than the normal text (GOV.UK 2020; NTR 2019). Larger inter-letter / character spacing (sometimes called tracking) improves readability. (In MS Word: Home - Font – Expand – Advanced – Spacing – Expanded – 0.8pt). Larger line spacing improves readability and should be proportional to inter-word spacing; 1.5 / 150% is preferable. Add extra space around headings and between paragraphs (NTR 2019). Keep designs clear, simple and clutter-free. (‘White space’ is great.) Page 12 of 39 Left align text, without justification. Avoid multiple columns (as used in newspapers). Lines should not be too long: 60 to 70 characters. Break up the text with regular section headings in long documents and include a table of contents. Images support meaning when chosen well. Illustrate your commitment to equality with images that include disabled people and show off your access provisions. All images should have a brief description underneath them, for visually impaired people using text readers. Do not put text over images. Where possible, or when the document will be in circulation for the publication for long periods of time, create an EasyRead version of the document, to make the information accessible to people with Learning Disabilities. Offer multiple formats of the information. Provide an option for the document in Word/Plain Text format and PDF format, this allows people to choose how they interact with the information. Consider providing brief videos of the text being read out. Consider providing BSL videos of text. Consider Sign-A-Long or Makaton videos of text for information relevant to communities that use these forms of communication. Always include information about disabled access within any space where an event is taking place (e.g. level access, lifts, toilets, hearing loops etc.) See Section 5 Event access for more information. Use active rather than passive voice. Be concise; avoid using long, dense paragraphs. Use short, simple sentences in a direct style. Use images to support text. Flow charts are ideal for explaining procedures. Pictograms and graphics can help to locate and support information in the text. Consider bullet points & numbering rather than continuous prose. Give instructions clearly. Avoid double negatives. Avoid abbreviations where possible; always provide the expanded form when first used. Provide a glossary of abbreviations and jargon. Use single colour backgrounds. Avoid background patterns or pictures and distracting surrounds. Use sufficient contrast levels between background and text. Use dark coloured text on a light background. Avoid green and red/pink, as these colours are difficult for those who have colour blindness. Consider alternatives to white backgrounds for paper, computer and visual aids such as whiteboards. White can appear too dazzling. Use cream or a soft pastel colour. Some dyslexic people will have their own colour preference. Page 13 of 39 With long documents, offer the document as a word file, electronically, so that readers can determine their own colour, size, spacing and contrast preferences. For colour blindness it is best to avoid these colour combinations (Collinge 2017): • Green and Red • Green and Brown • Blue and Purple • Green and Blue • Light Green and Yellow • Blue and Grey • Green and Grey • Green and Black Other colour combinations that can be difficult: • Yellow and Purple • White writing on bright backgrounds • White writing on pale backgrounds Photoshop can simulate the experience of viewing a document with colour blindness with these two proofing commands: View > Proof Setup > Color Blindness - Protanopia Type View > Proof Setup > Color Blindness - Deuteranopia Type Gloss finish on paper is often too reflective, and sheen can be too, so use matt. Paper should be thick enough to prevent the other side showing through. Page 14 of 39 This is a summary, further details of examples, standards, and implementation guidance is available from the W3C WAI web pages. Web accessibility relies on several components that work together. Some of these include: Web content - refers to any part of a website, including text, images, forms, and multimedia, as well as any markup code, scripts, applications, and such. User agents - software that people use to access web content, including desktop graphical browsers, voice browsers, mobile phone browsers, multimedia players, plug-ins, and some assistive technologies. Authoring tools - software or services that people use to produce web content, including code editors, document conversion tools, content management systems, blogs, database scripts, and other tools. • Short equivalents for images, including icons, buttons, and graphics • Description of data represented on charts, diagrams, and illustrations • Brief descriptions of non-text content such as audio and video files • Labels for form controls, input, and other user interface components • Text transcripts and captions for audio content, such as recordings of a radio interview • Audio descriptions, which are narrations to describe important visual details in a video • Sign language interpretation of audio content, including relevant auditory experiences (see section 5.1). • Headings, lists, tables, input fields, and content structures are marked-up properly • Sequences of information or instructions are independent of any presentation Page 15 of 39 • Browsers and assistive technologies provide settings to customize the presentation • Colour is not used as the only way of conveying information or identifying content • Default foreground and background colour combinations provide sufficient contrast • When users resize text up to 400% or change text spacing, no information is lost • Text reflows in small windows (“viewports”) and when users make the text larger • Images of text are resizable, replaced with actual text, or avoided where possible • Users can pause, stop, or adjust the volume of audio that is played on a website • Background audio is low or can be turned off, to avoid interference or distraction Many people do not use the mouse and rely on the keyboard to interact with the Web. This requires keyboard access to all functionality, including form controls, input, and other user interface components. Keyboard accessibility includes: • All functionality that is available by mouse is also available by keyboard • Keyboard focus does not get trapped in any part of the content • Web browsers, authoring tools, and other tools provide keyboard support Some people need more time than others to read and use the content. For instance, some people require more time to type text, understand instructions, operate controls, or to otherwise complete tasks on a website. Examples of providing enough time include providing mechanisms to: • Stop, extend, or adjust time limits, except where necessary • Pause, stop, or hide moving, blinking, or scrolling content • Postpone or suppress interruptions, except where necessary • Re-authenticate when a session expires without losing data Content that flashes at certain rates or patterns can cause photosensitive reactions, including seizures. Flashing content is ideally avoided entirely or only used in a way that Page 16 of 39 does not cause known risks. Also, animations and moving content can cause discomfort and physical reactions. Examples of avoiding causing seizures and physical reactions: • Do not include content that flashes at particular rates and patterns • Warn users before flashing content is presented, and provide alternatives • Provide mechanisms to switch off animations, unless they are essential Well organized content helps users to orient themselves and to navigate effectively. Such content includes: • Pages have clear titles and are organized using descriptive section headings • There is more than one way to find relevant pages within a set of web pages • Users are informed about their current location within a set of related pages • There are ways to bypass blocks of content that are repeated on multiple pages • The keyboard focus is visible, and the focus order follows a meaningful sequence • The purpose of a link is evident, ideally even when the link is viewed on its own Input modalities beyond keyboard, such as touch activation, voice recognition (speech input), and gestures make content easier to use for many people. Yet not everyone can use each of these input modalities, and to the same degree. Particular design considerations maximize the benefit of these input modalities. This includes: • Gestures that require dexterity or fine movement have alternatives that do not require high dexterity • Components are designed to avoid accidental activation, for example by providing undo functionality • Labels presented to users match corresponding object names in the code, to support activation by voice • Functionality that is activated by movement can also be activated through user interface components • Buttons, links, and other active components are large enough to make them easier to activate by touch Understandable information and user interface 4.3.6 Text is readable and understandable Content authors need to ensure that text content is readable and understandable to the broadest audience possible, including when it is read aloud by text-to-speech. Such content includes: Page 17 of 39 • Identifying the primary language of a web page, such as Arabic, Dutch, or Korean • Identifying the language of text passages, phrases, or other parts of a web page • Providing definitions for any unusual words, phrases, idioms, and abbreviations • Using the clearest and simplest language possible, or providing simplified versions • Consider providing Plain Language Summaries or Easy Read options (FPLD 2023) Many people rely on predictable user interfaces and are disoriented or distracted by inconsistent appearance or behaviour. Examples of making content more predictable include: • Navigation mechanisms that are repeated on multiple pages appear in the same place each time • User interface components that are repeated on web pages have the same labels each time • Significant changes on a web page do not happen without the consent of the user Forms and other interaction can be confusing or difficult to use for many people, and, as a result, they may be more likely to make mistakes. Examples of helping users to avoid and correct mistakes include: • Descriptive instructions, error messages, and suggestions for correction • Context-sensitive help for more complex functionality and interaction • Opportunity to review, correct, or reverse submissions if necessary Robust content is compatible with different browsers, assistive technologies, and other user agents. We genuinely believe that anyone can work in science. We believe that having a diverse workforce enhances the quality and utility of the science created. The core workplace of science is the laboratory. In these guidelines “Labs" refers to laboratories, manufacturing and production lines, engineering facilities, etc. “Scientists” refers to scientists, technologists, engineers, mathematicians, and healthcare professionals etc. “Disabled” relates to people who are disabled, D/deaf, or have long term health conditions (both physical and mental), illnesses, or injuries, which have a significant impact on their ability to carry out everyday tasks. The aim was to create a set of documents that would provide a pragmatic and useful guide on to how to create an accessible lab workplace. We wished to accumulate relevant guidelines for lab contexts, edit them for relevancy, expand them in order to be as 8omprehensive as possible, and share them with the scientific community. The guidelines are mostly created from previously published work, which we cite. We wanted to provide guidelines for the whole of the lab work ecosystem, and to consider all types of impairments and disabilities. 1 Structural access – physical design of laboratory and fixed equipment (e.g., hoods, sinks etc.) 2 Equipment access – design and use of movable equipment (e.g., microscopes, centrifuges, PCR machines etc.) 3 Protocol access – adaptation of lab protocols to accommodate access needs (e.g., seated working, evacuation protocols, lone working etc.) 4 Dissemination access – work done in laboratories must be shared with the wider world. Access issues can be encountered in consultation and dissemination events, meetings, conferences, the publication of work on web pages and in journal articles. Page 36 of 39 5 General working practices access – adaptation of usual HR and working practices (e.g., part time or flexible hours), assisting disabled staff to access to relevant benefits, accessible transport and parking etc. A significant proportion of the Access All Areas in Labs team have disabilities themselves, with lived experience of impairments in mobility, vision, stamina, dexterity, mental wellbeing, cognitive focus, and a range of neurodiversities. They have worked in microbiological, immunological, engineering, electronic, clinical trial, and pharmacy settings as students, researchers, principal investigators, technicians, and administrators. We searched scientific databases (MEDLINE, EMBASE); grey literature; professional magazines; online resources; relevant charities and trade unions; centres for disability studies; consultants that support disabled researchers and employers. We snowballed contacts and resources from the originally identified literature. We also conducted a survey of people with an interest in lab access about barriers and solutions to lab access (Deane 2023a) along with a set of case study interviews examining solutions to lab access (AAAiLabs 2023). We identified a key guideline or two at the start of the creation of each of our guidelines. This would then be combined with information from other guidelines, data from the survey and case studies, and combined with the team’s lived expertise to allow us to provide comprehensive guidelines with exemplars of implementation solutions across a range of settings and impairments.
